div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

At this season of the year everyone seems to be on the move, whether on business or pleasure bent. ' Even the most indefatigable worker finds time for a sojourn, more or less prolonged, of recreation in the country or by the seaside. This year this is more particu- larly the case, for the weather in the earlier part of the summer, having proved so un- seasonably wet and cold, many people have delayed their annual holiday as late as pos- sible in the hopes of brighter days, and there is consequently a pretty general exodus from town, and the principal railway stations are full of family parties, en route in many

instantes for north of the Tweed. The days are now long, reckoned among the annals of the past, when Englishwomen 'were noted for the shabbiness and unbecoming nature of their 'toilette when travelling, for with the advance of time has come a corresponding Stride in sartorial matters, with the result that .many exceedingly smart gowns are to be 'seen en route for the various watering- places. .There are, of course, and I suppose evrei will be, some mistaken individuals who will persist in appearing in soiled finery 'When travelling; but these, 1 fancy, are
f3rtunately_ becoming each season !ei:v-er. in

mumber. It is really quite an insight into ilife and character to spend an hour at one of the large railway termini watching the passengers who in every variety of costume hurry to and fro on the various platforms. The toilette depicted is one designed for 'comfort as well as smartness•when travelling, and is made of reddish-brown serge, with a trim coatee, and a skirt which clears the ground all round. Dust and dirt does not show on this material, and .the narrow pip- ings of red used on it give a becoming warmth. The blouse worn with it is of thin silk spotted with black and finished at the throat by a lace collar and dull red stock tie. Wei are often much -too careless in
FROCK;

regard to the correct arrangement of our collar and •tie, in which we are set a truly good example by the Parisienne, who will not only adjust her silk and lawn cravat to a nicety in a large bow or long ends in front, but pays equally careful attention to her waistband.

In -spite of the continued influx of fashion- able materials which each ensuing season brings in its train, there is one variety which never 'loses -its place in popular estimation— namely, serge, which for really good hard rough and ready wear has not a rival. In stormy or fine •weather it always looks well, and if a costume of this materidl is properly cut to commence with, it will stand all the hard wear •consequent on boating or picnic expeditions in all -sorts of circumstances and yet retain -a look of smartness -unknown to any other -fabric. The simple frock sketched is of navy blue unshrinkable serge, and is suited to the ,angular outlines of a girl .from twelve to fifteen years of age. The bodice is plain, yet :sufficiently full in front, a box

pleat extending down the front being stitched flat for four or five inches on the chest, from where the material is allowed to remain full to the waist, where it is again caught in. The sleeves are small bishops, caught into a tight cuff at the wrists, and the skirt, which is shaped so as to have a spring towards the hem, is trimmed only by the tucks. The waist is finished by a "sash of bright red washing silk tied in a bow at the back of the waist, the ends finished by a silk fringe. To complete this ideal frock for a young girl is added a narrow lawn turnover collar and a red silk cravat at the throat, and a soft flexible straw hat something between a• sailor and a Panama in shape and material, round the crown of which a navy blue silk scarf with the fringed ends embroidered in red silk is carelessly knotted.

Scarlet has always 'a, fasanation for the French leaders of fashion, and the coatee depicted is of linen of this colour, with a turnover white collar edged with coarse white lace as a finish. A smart coatee of this style will often be found useful for wear with a' skirt to Match, or will contrast pleasantly with one of holland colour ,or even navy blue. Another useful coatee of the same kind is made in white cloth, with a red or blue cloth taffeta collar finished with sets of gold buttons, or bordered with a narrow galon d'or. - Equally smart are the little coats made. loose and double-breasted in very much the same fashion as a reefer coat, only with, the- addition of triple shoulder capes COQUBTTII4

The Panama Hat.—lt will not be a great misfOrtune if the Panama hat makes a final exist with the,dismal summer of 1903. They have never been so much affected by women as by men, but whereas the girl can trim and ornament her Panama with ribbons, the man cannot. It is just simply a flop covering. Not one in twenty can wear them to advantage, and to many they give an appearance not very dissimilar from a newly tied-down jampot. Nevertheless they are greatly affected by men at the seaside, especially when the sun has shone quite often, perhaps two or three times in the day. Fashions in boots and shoes.,—The shortened skirt has been hailed with delight by the bootmakers to whom it has brought many orders for new footgear which would otherwise not have been wanted. It is pretty certain that as soon as the holiday season is over we shall be compelled to resume the skirt which has to be lifted from the pavements, but the shortened dress has had the effect of improving the general style and choice of footgear. Our own makers at last recognise that boots must be made to fit, instead of taking it for granted that the foot must fit the boot, and they now turn out footgear equally as well fitting and finished as the best American boots and shoes. The long vamp, and ridicu- lously pointed toe, which the Americans made all the fashion, have however been done to death, and' this style is being discarded not only in this country, but also by i American women. After that he was allowed to manipulate the levers, change the speeds, put on the brake, stop the car, and re-start it, till he appeared to have a thorough grasp of tha subject. He thought the whole thing ridicu lously easy, till Riley. pointed out that the had just begun to learn his business, and that oni a complete knowledge of the machinery would fit him to cope with any emergency or acci- dent.

However, the iron had entered into Wal• royd's soul, and he gloried in his new found strength. The rush of the air and the huru of the machinery were music to him. He saw now that being driven in a car was. nothing to the driving of it. It was the fact of controlling and guiding sixteen horse powei of machinery that appealed to him. Already he saw infinite possibilities. In less than two and a half hours they were fifty miles away from Garth, and were in the very heart of the mountains. Some of the gradients had been one in five, and they had climbed over one road to a height of two thousand feet. They stopped at a small inn, and had some bread and cheese and beer—all that the place could provide. The swift run through the mountain air had made them both as ravenous as wolves. But Riley would only allow a hurried meal. It was after hall past five and if they were to be back in time to dress for dinner, he would have to get every ounce of power out of the machine. He expressed •his intention of driving himself, and Walroyd was not sorry to give up the control. The latter was not used to the strain, and he found that his hands were a 'bit shaky and that his eyes ached painfully. They sped through the purple mountains towards the sunset. The western sky flamed with gold, and behind them the light clouds hung like rosy feathers against the blue of the heavens. It was the loneliest part 4of Wales, and nothing could be seen but the interminable ranges of the hills, clothed with wood at the bases; and covered with rock and heather at their summits. But the wild and rugged grandeur of the scenery passed by unnoticed by the occupants of the car. They crawled up the long slopes and spun down the long descents without V.ving a thought to what lay on either side of chem. All Riley's attention was required for the car, which he was dr;wing at a reckless speed, and Walroyd occupied his time in telling his companion about the long list of the Cardiganshire murders, and of the terror which lay over the whole countryside.

" S'pose you're armed," Riley said, when Walroyd ,came to the end of the narrative. " I ain't. I didn't reckon I'd want a gun in this part of the world." "Yes, I'm armed," Walroyd replied, putting his hand to ht pocket. " But I don't think, we'll need to .shoo t if ,ve meet Tredeg.ar. He won't run his head Agninit this car." " I dunno," Riley answered. "We go pretty slowly up soine•of these hills, and he Might board us. I r,tckon from all you say he might twist our.. net..ks if you didn't plug him."

At last they reached the eastern side of the hills above Llynglas. This was the steepest gradient of the -vilot journey. The road rose in a straight line from the bottom to the F nmmit, without a curve or angle to lessen the steepness- of the ascent. On either side of it vere woods of Oak and larch. Sheltered iron the western gales, these trees had grown to a greater height and breadth than their less fortunate comrades on the western slopes 'over T.,1:,-aglas. Even in the middle of surnmer the suit never shone on this side of the hill after four o'clock, and on this particular evening. late in the autumn, it was almost in darkness, though_ the too of the range behind glowed with idol. Where the road- passed over the summit, the trees were silhouetted gains the the crimson sky, but at the foot there '.vas bottling but dull grey twilight. They ascended on the lowest speed, slowly but surely, though the engine seemed to require a little- coaxing, and there was a faint squeak in the machinery that Riley was not at all pleased to hear.

Whe'n they were half way up the slope the figure of a man showed dark against the sky at the top of the hill. Then it appeared to descend on the other side, and vanished out of sight. 'Riley glanced nervously at Wal- royd. His mind was full of the stories he had just heard. "Might board us now, eh ? " he said. " Wouldn't get hurt by the car. I reckon." . Walroyd smiled, .and pulling out his revolver, slid it back into his pocket. Riley seetur.xl reassured. , .
"You were always handy with your gun, PeV.rson," he said.

, "I only wish I had a chance," - Walroyd replied grimly. At last they retched the summit, and the broad panorama of sea. and marsh lay before them. The sun had sunk to a half ball of red fire, and a mist'was rising from the earth and sea. Riley stopped the car on a piece of level ground at the tOp. The engines began to thr,b and rattle. " Guess I'll light the lamps," he said. "We shall reed them through these trees, and it'll'be ( -irk enough before we are home." descended from the car, and struck a match. A steady breeze was blowing off the sLa and it came strongly over the top of the hill. The mateh went out. • Riley swore under his breath, and retreated behind the shelter of the car. Walroyd leant forward and opened the front of the lamps. Neither man saw a dusky figure creep out of the woods and crouch in the shadows by the side of the wood.

Then suddenly something sprang out from the darkness, and grasped Riley in an iron embrace. Walroyd's .hand went to his pocket m.nd he leaned back over the seat with the revolver in his. hand. An enormous figure stool out in the last glow of the sunset. It was brown from ,head. to foot, and apparently covered with a mass of tawny hair. Walroyd saw that it was 'certainly not Emrys Tredegar. Riley's black figure wriggled like a stoat in a trap. • • Shoot," he yelled; "for God's sake
-shoot."

Walrovcl levelled his revolver. Then Le miled grimly, and placing the weapon on the pulled a lever towards him. The car b---•gan to move slowly forward. Riley clutched at it with one hand, but it slid from his grasp. Then he screamed like a wounded animal.

The car shot forward over the brow of the hill. Two hundred yards down the slope Walroyd applied the brakes, and brought . it to a dead stop. He looked back and saw nothing. Then,. he heard a long wail of agony. He raised his revolver and fired six shots into the air.. Then he released the brakes, and the machine dropped down the slope :ike a falling stone,
BY HARRIS BURLAND, Atrusoß os'bAcoaßAlrrc.

services on her behalf.. He 'read also of the death of Dennis Riley, and how lohn Walroyd had been carried down the hill on a runaway rector car, which in his ignorance he could neither stop nor control, and how he had, at risk of loosing the steering wheel, leant over the back and fired every barrel of his revolver at the murderer% There was a graphic account of the' swift run down the hill in the dark, and a realistic picture of the man who knew nothing of motor cars, steering the machine through' the dusk at the rate of sixty miles an hour. Eye- witnesses in Trethol described how he haq shot past them like an arrow, trying out to them to go to the top of the hill and save a man from death. But this new. horror made only a slight impression on Tredegar's mind. Mavanwy occupied all his thoughts. Perhaps at that very moment she was lying dead. Indeed it scarcely seemed possible. that she could be alive after all these days. He hardly dared to think oif how she might eventually be found. For the .last twelve hours he had, been in a living, hell, and they had left a deeper mark on his 'face and character than all the past months of suffering and misery. His face was almost bloodless, and the lines on it were such as might have been graven ;on the face of an invalid after years of bodily agony. All through the long night .he had lain on the rattling lolling truck, and faced the horrible thoughts which had crowded round him in the darkness, like fiends waiting to tear him in pieces. No single ray of hope had pierced the gloom. Yet he had resolved to find Mavanwy—dead or alive—and his own safety was nothing to him. If she were dead, 'he would avenge her—and avenge her terribly. The lust of blood was in his soul, and he swore that even the innocent should suffer, if Mavanwy were dead. He crept unobserved from the railway line to the Llynglas 'woods. Before he started he had taken the precaution of filling all his pockets with food, and had even provided himself With a knapsack, which was stuffed to bursting point with bread and cold bacon and cheese. He did not know how long it would be before he could enter .a shop and purchase anything. But he had not been able to quench his thirst for twenty-four hours. His mouth and throat were dry and burning. He made his way straight to the little waterfall in the woods, and lying down, I drank deeply. When he had satisfied 'lris craving, -he ate some bread and cheese, took another draught of water from the stream, and set off through the woods in the darkness. He had made up his mind to skirt the open bog, and walk round by the hills and woods to the Plas Tredegar. There, if anywhere, he expected to find some traces of the monster—the homicidal maniac • that he now . believed him to be. It was even possible that he might get to close quarters with this half human beast. But first he must find Mavanwy---alive or dead.—and then he could deal with the "• Cardiganshire Terror" as the South Wales Doily News had termed it. He almost smiled as he thought of the phrase. It had been applied to himself, as the sup- posed murderer. • He took two hours to reach the Tredegar woods. The moon was now up, but only a faint grey light filtered through the leaves overhead. It • was difficult to see even the trunks of the trees, and it took much time and many fruitle4s searches to discover the shaft of the old Tredegar mine. It was very quiet in the heart of the wood, and his foot- steps seemed to crash in the silence. An owl hooted mournfully in the distance. But no other live thing seemed to be awake. At last, after a long and tiring search, Tredegar came to the foot of the mound, and retracing his steps a few yards, discovered thy remnants of the web. His heart sank as' he fingered the severed cords. "They have evidently searched the wood thoroughly,- he said to himself, "and have found nothing —but this." He decided, however, to pass the night in the wood, and trust to fortune to reward his patience. He lay down in the shelter of some undergrowth close to the edge of the clearing, lit his pipe, and kept his eyes fixed on the tall grey mound that rose before him in the moon- light. He watched for an hour and saw nothing except the slim body of a fox slinking across the shale towards the Plas Tredegar. Then at last he heard a faint sound in the distance, as though something were moving stealthily through the wood. It was not continuous, but every now and then a twig would snap or a stone rattle, or there would be the swish of boughs being brushed aside. The noises came nearer and nearer, till at last he could judge the direction from whence they came. In a few minutes' time a gigantic figure crept on all fours out of the wood into the moonlight, and began to scale the mound. Tredegar's heart stood still and every muscle in his great body quivered. He longed to rush from his hiding place, and grapple with this loathsome creature and tear it limb .from limb. He swiftly counted up the number of its victims. Ten had already died in its grasp, and he shuddered as he thought that one more might yet be added to the list. He cursed the fate that had up to then pre- vented it from attacking him. He alone, of all the men in the district, could have met it on equal terms, and laughed at its ferocious strength. And as he saw it creeping up the bank of shale towards the mouth of the shaft he could hardly keep himself from following it and forcing it to fight for its life. He restrained himself, however. His busi- ness was to discover what had happened to Mavanwy-, and not to destroy this monster till it had given him some clue to her fate. He watched it crawl to the top of the mound, for all the world like some gigantic crab or spider. There was something uncanny in this creature terrorising the whole of a county. A single well aimed shot from a rifle or a gun would have killed it, and its gigantic strength would have availed it nothing. But it had appeared to bear a charmed life,, or else fortune had been with it, and its lack of ' intelligence had called forth the pity of the ' gods. In half a dozen instances it ought, in all human probability, to have been killed. But everything had fought on its side, and it still lived. Tredegar watched it crawl to a spot close to the mouth of the shaft and begin to scratch furiously among the stones. Then he saw it pull out something, and carry it to the top of the mound. Then it again stopped and flung a fe.w bits of, slate down the slope. -A few moments afterwards it disappeared. He watched for five minutes and then crept cautiously up the bank. When he reached the summit he saw to his surprise that the end .of a steel bar was protrnding from the ground, and that a rope was attached to it and that the rope trailed over the, edge of the ; shaft and disappeared into blackness. He listened for a minute or two, but heard nothing except the drip-drip of water down the walls of the shaft. The rope hung slack, and it was evident that whatever had de- scended by it had reached the bottom. Re offered up a silent prayer of thanks to Heaven. The murderer -was in a trap. Tredegar had only to 'decide whether to wait till it appeared .once more above ground, co. to follow it into the bowels of the earth. He resolved to follow it, and swinging ' himself to the edge of the shaft, let himSelt. down hand over hand till he reached the bottom and stood ankle-deep in the water. Then he looked up, and saw a faint square of dark blue above him. Half a dozen stars glowed clear and bright in the sky, as though i seen through a long telescope. He groped his way round the walls till he came to an open- ing. He remembered it well. More than once

div.head: CHAPTER XXI. THE OLD TREDEGAR LEAD MINI.
div.p: CHAPTER XXI. THE OLD TREDEGAR LEAD MINI.

WHEN Tredegar dropped off the luggage train, as it slowed down into 'Trethol Junction, the last light of day was glowing in the western horizon. He had been twenty-four hours .in the truck, and had spent half the time . in a siding thirty miles south of his destination. He had no clear conception of how he should act. He was a hunted man, and could not .openly join any rescue party, or give any asstance • in the search for Ma vanwy. Before he left Cardiff he had bought an evening paper, and had gathered from its columns that the missing girl had not yet been found, though every inch of the neigh- bourhood had been scoured, and every man within a- radius _ol_ ten miles had given his

div.p: In his boyhood he had braved the ghostly terror of the dead miners, and had descended with a companion to the first passage of the old workings. They had never ventured very far into the mine, but he recollected that the experience had been glorious and unique, an* that those days had been tun tc the brim v., ith the wild adventures that the) had imagined in such weird and unconven tional surroundings. He moved cautiously down the tunnel, keeping one hand on the slimy wall, and on the alert to catch the faintest sound. But he could hear nothing save the beating of his own heart and the light scrape of his boots on the rock under his feet. He had a full box of wax matches in his pocket, but was afraid to strike one for fear of disclosing his presence. As far as he remembered, the tunnel ran for at least three hundred yards without join- ing any other passages, and he was in no danger of taking the wrong path. Then came the place where the great fall of rock had occurred in 1873. He had neye.r penetrated beyond that fatal spot. At last his feet struck against a piece of loose rock lying on the floor of te tunnel, and he knew that he had reachecs rue scene of the disaster. In a few seconds a pile of debris breast-high lay in his path. He stopped and lit a match. It was hopeless to try and find his way any further without light. The feeble yellow flame showed a great mass of fallen rock stretching as far as the eye could reach. The roof above was ten feet higher than in the rest of the tunnel, and the floor was raised to within three feet of it. It had taken :a hundred men ten days to move that top layer of rock and find a way into the workings two hundred yards beyond. Most of the victims had been starved to death. But some had been taken from the debris, and two had never been found. Tre- degar shuddered as he thought that even then their bodies might be lying under those thou- sands of tons of slate. He crawled to the top of the heap, and . moved along on his hands and knees. In places he had to lie down and wriggle along. He was sparing with his matches, and pro- ceeded for the most part in the darkness. He hoped he would .not meet his quarry, till he had passed the scene of the disaster. It would have been an awkward place for a fight to the death. At last, however, he came to the end of his arduous task, and lit another match to accomplish his descent. As he did so, some- thing large and brown moved swiftly from under the shadow of a great mass- of slate, and disappeared in the darkness beyond. Tredegar picked up a heavy stone and hurled it after the retreating figure. He heard his missile clatter against the wall of the tunnel. Then he descended to the level, and started off in pursuit. But the chase was hopeless from the first. Little tunnels began to diverge 'a every direction. Every now and ther e stopped and lit a match. More than once he found himself in some large cliarnlyn- hollowed out from the rock, and half a dozen passages led from it in various directions. The pursuit was bewildering. In less than five minutes he had lost all traces of the thing he -pursued, and he listened in vain for any sound of foot- steps. Then he began to realise that his own posi- tion was not a very cheerful one. He had no idea of tile route he had taken. In his eagerness he had forgotten to mark out a path by which he might return. He was lost in a labyrinth of passages, and with no light but such as he could get from the fitful flare of a few matches.

Tredegar's purpose, however, was strong, and he thought little of his own danger. He wag amply provided with food, and water dripped from every crevice in the rock. He was determined to explore the place till starvation stared him in the face. Here, at any rate, was the thing he sought. It might escape him, but at least he Would do his best to run it to earth. It was also possible that Mavanwy might be somewhere in these labyrinthine depths. But he thoUght in his own heart that he should find her dead. And so, hour after hour, he blundered on through the silence and the gloom, every now and then returning to the same spot, but never once corning back to the place where he had crossed the fallen rock. He neither saw nor heard .anything, His stock of matches was almost exhausted, and he felt sick and tired. The atmosphere of the mine was none too good. At last he resolved to sit down and have something to eat. _ _ _ .

„... He made a hearty meal off bread and bacon. He had to tear off pieces of the latter with his teeth, as he had forgotten to bring a knife with him. But, for all that, he enjoyed the food, which put fresh strength into his weary brain and body. ° When he had finished, he groped his, way once more through the black- ness.

In half an hour's time he came to a passage Which seemed to descend. When he had proceeded along it for about two hundred yards, it turned suddenly to the left, and as he crept Cautiously round' the corner he saw a faint glow of light in the distance. He stopped and listened, but he could hear nothing. He took off his boots, and moved silently along the, rocky floor. When he was within twenty yards of the light he saw that it came from the side of the rock, and seemed like the light of a candle. But, if so, the candle itself was hid from observation, either in a niche or round another corner. Then suddenly his foot went splash into a pool of water several inches deep, and the noise reverberated down the passages. Al- most simultaneously the light went out. He cursed his carelessness, and, running swiftly -forward, came to a corner. Some- thing stirred as he turned to the right, and he thought he heard the sound of breathing. He stretched out his arm, and, touching the wall, swept it lightly with his fingers as he moved. Then he encountered some hair, and at the same time a piercing shriek rang through the vault of the passage, and there was the thud of a falling body, and then silence. _ _ _
He struck a match, and saw a huddled heap at his feet. He leant down, and looked at the face. It was Mavanwy Morgan I
CHAPTER XXII. THE PALACE OF THE DEAD.

TREDEGAR found a lantern on the floor by her side, and, lighting it, placed it on a ledge of rock. He hurried back to the pool he had just put his foot into, and filling his sailor's cap with water, dashed some in the. face ol the unconscious girl.. Then he . fell on his knees and kissed her forehead. In a few minutes she opened her eyes and shivered. Then she stared at him, as though she could hardly believe her senses, and gave a little cry of surprise. " Emrys," she said, sitting up, and brushing back the wet hair from her face. " Emrys ! Oh, thank God you have come to me! But how--4 thought you had left England ? I, do not understand. And my father ?" And she looked eagerly into his face. "He is dead 1" Tredegar replied, in a low voice. •` I saw it in the papers. I saw, too, that you were missing. Do you think I could go after that ? I returned at once ; the paper was four days old when .I saw it. Thank God I have come in time, and that I have found you. I thought—l hardly dared to hope--!' "How long have I been here ?" she broke in, struggling to her feet. "I have lost all count of time. It has been an endless night —hour after hour of darkness and fear. I think I should have killed myself if I had had the means to do so. Ido not know where I am. I have wandered- miles and miles in this tomb, seeking .for some glimmer of light. Oh, it has been awful !" And she buried" her face in her hands.
Tredegar stepped towards her and made as though he would take her in his arms and shield • her from all the terrors she had imagined. But she shrank from 'him, and looked a 4 him piteously. "Al]

"No, .Emrys- ," she said, faintly that is past I But where am I?" "You are in the old Tredegar lead mine," he answered, coldly. " The shaft is in the woods by the house." And he told her lion he had followed the murderer and lost his way in the darkness,. And you, Mavanwv ?"

The MAYOR: On this particular occasion I wasn't at the committee meeting. Councillor PEMBERTON proceeded to refer to the terms of the contract with Mr. C. W. Davenport and dissented from the Town Clerk's ruling that the Corpor- ation had broken the contract by taking possession of the work before its oompletion. He would like to ask through the Mayor the following question of the Town Clerk: Is the contract of Lawson's broken because we have taken possession of No. 1 shaft? The MAXOR: This question does not arise out of the minutes. If you wish to make this inquiry you must give notice of it. _

Counci'llor fiORROCKS seconded the amendment. Councillor JOHN EVANS said Mr. Pemberton had got a wrong apprehension about Mr. Barron. Mr. Barron's work was not complete. An appointment was offered to Mr. Barron before the work was finished and he was allowed to go. This was the work Mr. Fletcher was allowed to work on.

Councillor PEMBERTON : Mr. Deas is mentioned as clerk of works in the contract. The TOWN CLERK pointed out that he did not advise the Council with reference to the contract. He advised upon the special facts which were submitted to him by the committee and these had reference to the payment of £lOO which Mr. Deas had certified the contractor was entitled to.

On the amendment being put, five members voted for it, namely: Councillors Dodds, Thornton, Pemberton, Lord and Horrocks. As in life, despite his public position, the late Marquis of Salisbury always held aloof from the public itself, so also was he aloof in death. By his own wish there was no public funeral of the great Premier: but he was quietly laid to rest in the Churchyard at his own home. Nor, as in the case of Mr. Gladstone, did the public rise unanimously .and demand one. To them Lord Salisbury was always a great politician and a splendid. .statesman, but his private personality was practically unknown. Indeed many of the most prominent men of the day had never ,exchanged a word with him; thus from his position of splendid isolation he seemed, from the very day of his retirement, to pass straight into history. Thus with the utmost simplicity and privacy the great statesman was laid to rest last Monday in the private burial-ground of the Cecils of Hatfield nine days after his death. The funeral would, in the ordinary course of events, have taken Place earlier, but was delayed to admit of the presgnce of Lord Edward Cecil, who missed the telegram summoning him back at Brindisi, and had to return all the way from Port Said. The Marquis of Salisbury was thus followed to the grave by all the mem- bers of his immediate family, and was laid beside the late Marchioness, who was his able helper for So many years. The private cemetery at Hatfield is a small oval of green, lying under the shadow of the old Church, of which Lord William Cecil is the rector. It is enclosed by a yew hedge and bordered by a bed of pink roses. It is entered by wrought-iron gates, which face the red brick walls of old Hatfield Palace, of which the old refectory is now used as stables. In one corner is the grave of ,the late Lord §alisbury's youngest daughter who died in infancy in 1867, and near it is the newly made grave of the Countess of Galloway, the late Premier's half - sister, who was
rPII

div.head: TOMB OF THE CECILS.
div.p: THE TOMB OF THE CECILS.

--- -- buried upon the day of his deiith. There is, also, the grave of Miss Alderson, the sister of the late Marchioness. The majority of the Cecil family lie buried in the private Chapel, Which is part of Hatfield Church. The tomb of the dead politician and his wife is of simple gray stone, unadorned• by any sculp- ture or carving, and he was carried from his ancestral home in a plain coffin of oak, cut upon the estate, as simple as any village Squire of no public note. Thus the last scene was in keeping with the habit of his whole life. Simultaneously a Memorial Service was held in Westminster Abbey, which was naturally a very distinguished , and repre- sentative gathering. The King, in his unavoidable absence, wis represented by his Lord Chamberlain, the Earl .of Clarendon, and the ,Prince of Wales by Lord Wenlock, and every member of the Royal Family who could not be present in person was repre- sented, as was the Kaiser and other crowned heads. It was a most distinguished congre- gation that did a last honour to the great Premier, and it was only second to the public funeral he did not desire. . •

THE NEW MEMBER FOR ARGYLL. At the General Election of 1900 Mr. Ains- worth, the new niember for Argyll, was beaten by the late member, Mr. D. N. Nicol, by 000 votes. This large minority he has now turned into a thumping majority of 1585. It is a curious fact that in 1900 7068 votes were polled and at this election 7066, a differ- ence in total of only two! It is claimed that the defeated candi- date, Mr. Chas. Stewart, was not so well known or popular in the constitu ency either as the late Mr. Nicol or Mr. Ainsworth. Whatever the cause, the Libe- rals in the con- stituency are naturally very delighted with the result. The new M.P. was
born in 1844,

and comes of a very wealthy Lancashire family. He is also interested in iron, mining, and other industries in West 'Cumberland. He was educated at University . College School and University 'College, London, and is an M.A. and LL.B. Of London. He is chairman of the Cleator and Workington Junction Railway, and until recently was colonel of the 3rd V.B. of the Border Regiment. Twice previously he has unsuccessfully contested elections. In 1886 he stood as a Gladstonian Liberal at Barrow- in-Furness against Mr. W. S. Caine; and, in 1900, as mentioned above, he was defeated in his .present constituency by the late member. Now, at last, his Parliamentary aspirations lave been crowned with success.

div.head: LONDON'S LATEST VEHICLE.
div.p: LONDON'S LATEST VEHICLE.
THE

London has long been looking out for a safe and suitable variation to the perilous hansom, Which is the present predominating vehicle in the streets of the metropolis. Accident fol- lowing accident on the wooden and asphalt roads have begun to engender a healthy dis- trust in this -type of public conveyance, and many experiments have been put in hand with view to an improvement. The latest prom- ise is the motor-hansom, and, whether- the Public like or dislike the genus motor, it will riot be long before they will' realise the ad- vantages of the self-propelled vehicle over the horse-drawn hansom with its attendant risks. In the new motors the driver will sit in front I)tweel the bonnet and the cab proper, which will corm a sort of covered tonneau. The

div.head: IMPUDENT OFFICE ROBBERY. -- Prisoner Sentenced.
div.p: THE IMPUDENT OFFICE ROBBERY. -- Prisoner Sentenced.

The extraordinary case of robbery which created some sensation in the town last week reached its final stage on Wednesday when the prisoner—Joseph Winsber a native of Bolton—received sentence. The charge against him was that of stealing a bag containing £66 from the'pay office of the Pearson and Knowles coal and Iron Company Limited at Bewsey. He pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner was origi- nally charged with stealing £73 10s but it had now been ascertained that the actual amount was £66. Mr. Talbot again detailed the facts of the case which were given in full in our last issue. Prisoner it will be remembered appropriated a bag of gold during the'temporary absence from the pay office of Mr. Price, the cashier. He after- wards had the effrontery to receive the wages due to him and leave the works.
When arrested the man had £3l 18s. 3d. in his pos- sessioa. The police had recovered 9s. 6d. from a com- panion of the prisoner and a balance of £4 13s. was unaccounted for.

The Chief Constable added that the prisoner had a criminal history. Besides two cases of theft which had been brought against him at Bolton he had been sentenced to. five years' penal servitude at Manchester Assizes for attempting to murder a policeman. He brought to the notice of the Bench the conduct of Parkes, to whom the prisoner's arrest was largely due; Mr. Ryder, who did what he was not obliged to do in promptlyhanding over the money paid for the watch and guard ; and also P.C. Terry, of the County Police, for his promptness. Mr. Birchall thankedall three on behalf of the Bench and the Chief Constable remarked that he wished then, was a fund from which he could remunerate Parkes for his assistance. However, the persons who had bane- fitted from hisaction might do something. Prisoner was sent to gaol for six months with hard labour.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
NORTHERN UNION.
LEIGH v. ST. HELENS,

This West Lancashire League match was played at Leigh on Tuesday evening, before 2,500 spectators. The play was not of an interesting character, few passing movements being seen. St. Helens beat Leigh in the scrummage, but the home forwards were best in the loose. St. Helens started against the slope, and after several minutes' even play Burgess l got injured and retired, but resumed after being off the field about eight minutes. Leigh atta,ckedas the result of a fine piece of play by Johnson, and St. Helens being penali9ed Moly- neux dropped a goal. Leigh had the best of the play for some time, and then Creerey intercepted a pass and ran close to the Leigh line, where Bennett brought him down. From the next scrummage the ball came out on the St. Helens side, and Pennington dodged over:and scored a smart try, Lee placing a goal. At the interval St. Helens led by Live points to two. On resuming Leigh attacked repeatedly for twenty minutes, and Molyneux just missed dropping a goal. Ganley almost got in twice, but the St. Helens tackling was wonderfullygood Towards the close Burgess again retired hurt. Leigh lacked scoring power, and St. Helens won by a goal and a try (five points) to a goal (two points).

div.head: NEW RUSSIAN VICEROY.
div.p: THE NEW RUSSIAN VICEROY.

There is no question that Russia has been particularly active dufing the last few weeks in politics, both European and Asiatic; and, though she has failed to embroil herself in a war, she has only just failed by the skin of her teeth. In Europe her diplomatic ielations have been with Turkey over the question of the
murder of the
Russian consul
at Monastir and the turbulent
state of the Bal-
kans ; and her represent at ion was a very
strong one,
backed both by
England and
Austria,
result was that
Turkey climbed down and ac- ceded in full to all the Russian demands. . This settled the Eur-
- VICE-ADMIRAL ALEXEIEFF. Opean temporarily at

anyrate. In the East the trouble with Japan took considerably more adjustment. Russian policy in the East has always been to spread through Asia to the coast, a course which is naturally menacing not only to Japan espe- cially, but also to England, and, to a lesser degree, to the other Powers; and her diplomacy, despite rebuffs from time to time, has made considerable progress. The recent announce- ment of the appointment of a "Viceroy of the East" is simply a step in the consolida-

- al a set poliCi. The ukase in question, signed by the Tsar, provided that the Amur district, which hfis hitherto been under a Gov- ernor-General. 11(1 the Kwantung territory should be merged into a special Viceroyalty under the above title. For this new post Vice-Admiral Alexeieff, the Tsar's personal aide-de-camp General, has been chosen, and he will shortly take up his important duties. In the first place he has been instructed to submit to the Tsar, for his Majesty's approval, pro- posals for the administration of the huge territory ovei which he is to assume jurisdic- tion. On :hest will hinge a good deal— possibly even the peace of Europe and Asia, and they will be anxiously awaited by diploma- tists. This appointment is undoubtedly a very important move in Eastern politics.

div.head: DICKENS'S BIRTHPLACE.
div.p: DICKENS'S BIRTHPLACE.

Probably no more popular or widely-read novelist has ever lived than Charles Dickens, whose books will be found in almost every house or cottage throughout the country, and he himself, now even more than ever in life, is a household word throughout the country. Nowadays there are Dickens' societies and Dickens' tours ; and few authors •either of the past orlr of the present show stronger signs of living in the future by their books. ' The life and history of Dickens as a man has often been written, and all the incidents of his career are familiar to the public. The various houses he

div.head: NO. 387, COMMERCIAL ROAD, PORTSMOUTH.
div.p: NO. 387, COMMERCIAL ROAD, PORTSMOUTH.

occupied, especially famous Gadshill, are well- known and frequently visited by his admirers; and it is seldom that one comes into the market. However:it is announced that before the end of this month there will be' sold the house in which the great novelist was born. It stands in Commercial Street, Portsmouth, and is a quiet, unpretentious, old-fashioned place. On the outside it bears no mark to show that it has associations superior to any of its neigh- hours; and it is to be hoped that the new purchaser will put a memorial tablet on the front of the house, recording its claim to fame, as has been done in the case of so many other great men of all sorts and descriptions, especially. in London. It would be a great pity„to let the birthplace' of such a notable Englishman fall into oblivion. Two schemes of redemption have been suggested. One is thrtt the Dickens Fellowship should provide the necessary money out of its funds, and the other that the municipality should find the money. In Portsmouth, the former scheme receives greater support, as it is felt that the matter is one more for a body like the Dickens Fellowshiy than for the local council.
The Examiner, Saturday, September 5, 1903.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SRPTEMBICH sth 1903.

WILL the Cabinet THE DUKE AND Council, now de- OTIIERS. layed,precipitate the fate of the Ministry or postpone it? There was a rumour on Tuesday that the DUKE of DEVONsHIRE was tired of the situation, and meant to put an eud to it by resign- ing. He would not resign alone, and his with- drawal would break up the Government. He has denied the rumour, and he may agree with some Ministerial partisans that the time for a crucial decision is not yet, that the evil day can be de- layed by the simple expedient of appointing a Royal Commission, and that there is no reason why Ministers should not meet Parliament next year, and pass a Midget on" current lines." This course implies a touching faith in the toughness of our party system. Tile "inquiry," so far as it has gone, has had the effect of tearing the Unionist party asunder. Mr. BALFOUR'S most vehement critics are of his own household. They openly revile him for playing Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S hand by evasions which violate their consciences. The frequent scenes in the House of Commons in the closing days of last session showed this feeling to be deep and bitter. But, hey presto! the magic balm of a Royal Commission is to heal these sore divisions, and everything is to go on as befoee. The ravaged bosoms of LORD HUGH CECIL and Mr. WINSTON CHuRcHrLL are to be soothed by the thought that the Royal Commission is patiently and laboriously going through the figures with which everybody by this time is tolerably familiar. Mr. RITCHIE is to bring in another budget sceupulously consistent with Free Trade, while Mr. CHAMBERLAIN sits in i smiling acquiescence, and the Birmingham leaflets litter the constituencies. Party ties are strong, but we doubt whether they could hold together such a figment of unity for another session. Besides even if the attention of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S Col- leagues could be distracted for a while from this• desolating question, what are they to think about? The English people, it is said, can take in only one idea at a time. Just now that idea is the taxation of food. If that is hurriedly ejected from the popular mind, what is to take its place? The operation of the Education Acts? The report of the War Commission? On neither, of these subjects, we surmise, do the Ministerial partisans desire to see the country concentrating its thoughts. If we can forget that Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN has proposed to put a tax on bread, how can

it profit the Government that we should remember all their gross incapacity in the c miduct of the war? That must be a fruitful theme of debate if Mr. BALFOUR should meet Parliament again as Prime Minister. He will have to explain why a Secretary for War who blunderel so scandalously as Lord LANSDOWNE can be fit to manage our foreign affairs. And he will have to explAin it, not merely to the Opposition, but more especiAlly to his nominal followers, whose distrust of the Government has become almost fanatical.

From no standpoint is the prospect agreeable for Mr. BALFOUR'S adherents, if there be any left. If the DUKE should resign, it may well be that, he sees no other way out of an incurably bad job. Even Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is reported to believe that his cause must be worse before it can 'ae better, that his party must taste the wholesome discipline of exclusion from office, and that it will suit him very well to make a Liberal Government the tar- get of his slings and arrows. That spectacle might revive the drooping spirits of , his friends, brit would it really work for Unionist cohesion? Years ago, in the thick of the Home Rule conflict, Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT had some lively passages of arms with two able opponents, whom he pleasantly designated as the Brothers Drenv. Professor A. V. DICEY and Mr. EDWARD DICEY rode into the battle like Castor and Pollux. Few writers did better work for the Unionist party; but now we per- ceive with concern that the brethren are divided. Mr. EDWARD DICEY has been rebuking the ULionist Free Traders because, he says, their defection from Mr. BALFOUR threatens to play into the hands of the iHome Rulers. But Pro- fessor DICEY, in the "Contemporary Review," puts the boot on the other leg. It is Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN'S policy ,of preferential tariffs, he declares which is dangerous both to Unionism and to Imperialism. He sees the Unionist elector con- fronted by this horribly perplexing dilemma : "Are you, if a Free Trader, to support a Unionist who is a friend to preferential tariffs; or are you, if a convinced Protectionist, to give your support to a Minister who is a firm adherent of Free Trade?" He admits that there are difficulties which may be evaded by "an ingenious speaker," but he warns Unionists that " when a popular audience is to be convinced nothing is so ineffective as subtlety or disingenuousness." Mr. EDWARD DICEY, how- ever, is neither subtle nor disingenuous, but in a perfectly straightforward way tells the Unionist Free Traders that their duty is to sink Free Trade and follow Mr. CHAMBERLAIN for the sake of the Union. Professor DICEY says that if this policy be adopted by the majority of the party the result must be "a vast diminution' of their authority and nnnabers, and a free hand to a Liberal Government to manipulate the new Irish Land Act as an instrument of Home Rule. It is one of the defeats of the Act that it provides no popular and representative Irish authority to stand between the State landlord and the ten ants. But Professor DICEY turns pale when he contem- plates "proposals to let Irish load bodies—bodies, it may be, filled with Irish Home Rulers—perform the duty of collecting the rents due to the State." This only shews that for the principle of devolu- tion in Irish • administration the stars in their courses are fighting. But Professor Die rx does not see the stars; he sees only the dire conse- quences of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S new adventure. Perhaps. his article will make the DUKE of DEVONSHIRE resign after all.

Education is a subject very much to the fore in Warrington just now. The columns of to-days " Examiner " bear ample evidence of this., To catalogue the events bearing on education whicq have taken place in the town during the past week requires considerable space. In the first place two excellent addresses on the subject were delivered on Sunday in connection with the anniversary of Silver-street elementuy school by Mr. E. J. Guest and Mr. C. E. Parker respectively. Then on Tuesday evening we had a discussion on the secondary school at the Town Council meet- ing. Two days later, the members of the War- rington Citizens' League held their first public meeting in support of passive resistance. Finally, occasion was taken last evening at the distri- bution of prizes in the Technical Institute to review educational work in Warrington. This quickening of interest in a matter of such vital importance to the future well-being of the town should bear fruit and we hope the result will be to remove the reproach which has been cast upon Warrington of being backward in providing effi- cient educational facilities. In the past there has been little enthusiasm for education amongst the community as a whole. This has been due to what Mr. Parker calls "the lack of appreciation of the great part that education can play in national ' progress and of the great mine of interest which is open to our children, even the poorest in the land." We are- now beginning to see more clearly what a great lever education has been in raising America and Germany to their present position in the industrial world and it behoves us to lose no further time in fetching up the leeway.:

For the first time, we believe, since the forma- tion of the Education Committee, there has been a discussion in the Town Council on the Committee's minutes. Three of the Non-Trading members took exception, at Tuesday's meeting, to the expenditure on secondary education. Councillor Lord opened,thelindictment by;charging Alderman Monks with estimating the expenditure under this head at £375, whereas is now stood at £1,748. He also objected to the appointment of a lecturer on school management and the theory of teaching, and, generally, charged the Education Committee with extravagance. Councillors Horrocks and Pemberton followed in similar vein, and if their's had been the only side of the case we should have had to conclude forthwith that the Education Committee was composed mostly of idiots capable only of wasting the ratepayers' money, and possess- ing no ability for the work they have to perform. Happily there i another point of view. It is unfortunate for the arguments of Messrs. Lord, Pemberton, and Horrocks that they are not educational experts. Even their most ardent admirers would hardly dub them such. As a mater of fact they are mere tyros in education, and when they begin to criticise it is not difficult to condemn them out of their own mouths. For advocating economy we do not blame them, but we think they are wasting the own and other people's time when they proceed argue that this appointment and that proposal are unnecessary. There are a good many men on the Education Committee who are authorities on their work and we look to these mon to raise the standard of efficiency in Warrington to something like what it should be in a County Borough of 70,000 inhabitants. Councillor Upson and Alderman Monks were b )th very convincing when they took up the defence. The former was particularly emphatic in asserting that they were doing no more than they were compelled to do by the Board of Education, and at the same time forecasted considerably greater expenditure in the event of a Liberal Govern- ment being returned at the next election. There is no doubt that with men like Mr. Lloyd ' George in the Cabinet, education in England would receive such an impetus as it has never felt before. The people 9f this town will have to reconcile themselves to expenditure on education, and cease to cavil. They have get a capable authority, and one, we believe, composed of men who will not rushlinto any extravagance. These men know as well as anybody that rates are hie', and they may be trusted to be mindful of this fact in the performance of their duties.

We have not heard much of "Passive Resistance" In Warrington but there is every reason to believe that the resisters will be much in evidence in the near future. A number of Nonconformists who challenge the moral corn- petenceof the Government to invade the realm of conscience are banding themselves together in a Citizens' League, and are determined no to pay the Education rate. The authorities will of course, put the screw on by means:of that ugly weapon—the distress warrant. This action will not daunt the resisters. They feel,as the Rev. J. Hirst Hrillowell very aptly summed up the whole situation, that" the duty of loyalty to con- science is higher and superior to the duty of sub- mission to the civil power." In resisting the law, the resisters are taking an extreme course but thby are convinced that the end justifies the means. The growth of such a movement pointedly calls attention to the grievances which the Edu- cation Act imposes upon Nonconformists, and to again quote Mr. Hollowell, "it is the shortest argument with the clergy."

The Town Council has taken another important step towards the holding of an inquiry into the trading question by appointing its three Commis- sioners to sit with the three nominees of the Non- Trading Association. We were opposed to the selection in an open Council for obvious reasons, but it was ultimately carried out in a perfectly satisfactory manner. True, it looked at one time, as though there would be some friction, when first one Councillor and then another put forward his ideal" three." There was even a touch of humour about the proceedings when Councillor Pierpoint, after explaining the difficulties in the way of his own acceptance of office, cast a search- ing eye over the members and mentioned first one and then another as candidates. They did not,by any means,trip over one another in order to "catch the speaker's eye." In fact,Alderman Fairclough's characteristically blunt statement that he" would not touch it" seemed to "fill the bill," so to speak. Somebody had to "touch it," however, and when Councillor Tinnion came forward with the proposal that the three Commissioners be Messrs. L,Green- ing, A. J. Jolley, and Thomas Birchall, J.P., he was hailed almost as a benefactor and these gentlemen were adopted. They have since accepted the appointment. We are sure they will have the confidence of the ratepayers. All three are gentlemen of established probity arid recognised experience in municipal and public life generally.

The public will now await with interest the appointment of the Non-Trading representatives. There has first to be the passing of sealed envelops between the two parties. Such a method seems hardly necessary, seeing that the names of the Corporation nominees are now public property. However, Councillor Dodds selected this course of procedure in the ,first instance and we suppose it will have to be carried out with due pomp and formality. The condition hardly seems to us "extremely unfair," as Alderman Bennett styles it. The Council were not obliged to make their selection in public,and theirlhaying done so does not affect the fairness of the Non-Traders' stipulation.

We have evidently not heard the last of the slack contracts by a great deal. on Tuesday Councillor Pemberton carried his motion "that a committee be appointed to inves-igate the last three slack contracts at Winwick and Dalph-lane." Alderman Francomb quite eagerly seconded this proposal and vouched for the willingness of the Water Committee to afford facilities for the fullest investigation. "This," as Councillor Tinnion remarked, "is a very proper spirit to meet any- thing of the kind." If the same spirit had been shown in regard to the great inquiry, it would probably have been held long ago, and the town by now have regained its normal pacific condition. Evidently some experience of inquiries is necessary for the cultivation of the"proper spirit."Councillors Craik, Pierpoint, Lord, Forshaw, and Pemberton have been appointed to inquire into the slack con- tracts, with instructions to proceed with the operations at once.

Although he failed to secure a seat on the Council, Mr. John Maginn has certainly won the hearts of the children of SG. John's Ward. The huge free picnic on Thursday was an event quite unique in the annals of the town and seemed to give unbounded delight to the youthful partici- pants. If all unsuccessful aspirants to municipal honours would follow Mr. Maginn's excellent example, elections would be almost as eagerly looked forward to as Walking Day V Mr. Maginn's suggestion that an annual outing be given to children who are never absent from school during the year is a good one, but we are afraid that there would not be such agreat demand for conveyances as was oxperienced on Thursday. At any rate the scheme is worth a trial, for a little encouragetnant goes a long way with school children.

There have been several curious mishaps due to the tram lines, and some followed by serious con- sequences. Another accident happened yesterday but fortunately it was of such a character that the onlookers were entitled to smile—and they fully availed themselves of the privilege. An ordiaary tradesman's van in charge of the usual small boy was jogging along Scotland road, when in crossing the tram-rails, the iron tyre of one of the wheels was jerked off. It immediately took advantage of its new-found liberty by bowling down the street "on its own." The van went on for a short dis- tance with the result that the tyreless wheel fell into several piecesland spokes were shed with pro- fuse liberality. Finally the van lay down sideways. In the meantime somebody captured the truant tyre and brought it back to the scene of the wreck where the youthful driver was busy gathering up the fragments.

"All their interests," writeslMr. Chamberla in, referring to the working classes, " depend upon full employment at fair wages," and he is con- fident that "this can only be permanently secured by some changes in our tariff systdm." According tothis,the;latest of the various authorised versions of the new gospel, we must turn to Protectionist countries to find" full employment at fair wages." But it so happens that last year in Germany was the worbt ever experienced from the point of view of the workmen. Thousands of Italians and Russians, who had found work there during the good times of 1897 to 1900,, were expelled by the police, and still there remained hundreds of thou- sands of Germans demanding employment in vain. As for the contention that Protection guarantees "fair wages," does Mr. Chamberlain imagine that the British worker has forgotten the colossal strike in the American coalfield only a year ago

div.head: &bares.
div.p: &bares.
The Assessment of the Royal Court Hotel.

A meeting of the Warring-ton Union Assessment Committee was held yesterday. Mr. A. J. Jolley presided. Mr. A. Browne appeared in support of an appeal by Mr. George Wright of the Royal. Court Hotel, Rylands-street. The assessment had been raised, he said, from £lO2 rateable .to -.£153 rateable, an increase of £1 in one bound. He did not know what the arguments were in favour of the increased assessment. Perhaps it might be on account of the trams stopping opposite this hotel. As a matter of fact the trams were of no benefit whatever to Mr. Wright, but on the other hand they prevented people from' coming into the house. On wet days, the doorway was blocked up by people waiting for the trams, and the trade of the house had not increased since the premises were re-built. Mr, Wright was bound to buy malt and hops from his land- lord, and he told him (Mr. Browne) that that was more expensive than other ways of brewing. (Laugh- ter.) He could not say anything more on that point. He submitted there was no justification for the increased assessment. Mr. Wright's returns were actually less than in the preceding year by 50 barrels. —The Clerk pointed out that it was not only an assessment for a house but an assessment for a brewery as well as a house. He wished the com- mittee to bear in mind all the circumstances and com- pare Bridge-street with other main streets in the town where the licensed houses were clustered together.— As a result of their deliberation in private, the Chair- man informed Mr. Browne that the committee could
ot make any change in the assessment.—Mr. Browne nave notice of appeal.
A GOOD RESOLUTION.—Wear ALE' TAYLOR'S Wonderful Boots.—Advt.

div.head: Failure of a Stockton Heath Builder.
div.p: Failure of a Stockton Heath Builder.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridoway, Charles Ellison Chappel,residing at:36,FairfielC-1 Rd,Stockton Heath and now carrying on business as a builder and contractor at Gaskell-street. but formerly carrying on the same business with a partner under the style or firm of " Chappel and Millington," , at 36, Fairfield-road, ar peared for his public examination. The bankrupt g statement of affairs showed that the liabilities were expected to rank at A:900 4s. id. The *assets were estimated to produce £125 9s. Bd., leaving a deficieneY of £774 14s. sd. The causes of failure, as alleged by bankrupt, were losses on contracts through under estimates and want of capital. In his statement to the assistant official receiver, the bankruPt stated that he commenced business about 91 years ago without capital. He attributed his deficiency to excess of liabilities over assets in De- cember 1901, £2l is 6d. ; bad debts £52 7s. 11d, anticipated loss on realisation of assets 5.20 18s. 6d. ; , loss by sale under distraint for rent is. Gd. ; losses on contracts .£546 ; and household and personal ex- Ipenditure in excess of income or profits .£lOO S. In answer to Mr. E. Johnson, assistant official receiver, witness stated that his losses on contracts were due to incompetency in estimating. He admitted that aboa 5 the time he suspended payment he handed over all unfinished contract to Mr. John Pemberton. Askeu why he showed this preference to Mr. Pemberton ova other creditors, witness said Mr. Pemberton wag friend of his and had lent him money. It was part of the arrangement with Mr. Pemberton that he (witness) should hand over the benefit in this contract to 'Mr' Pemberton. He considered that the benefit in then" finished contract was a little over ,£lOO. the time he agreed to hand over the cull:, tract, Mr. Pemberton advanced him •t:'1" to pay wages. He had previously borrowed sums 4 money from Mr. Pemberton amounting to a further sum of about £6o.—The Assistant Official ReceiveF, asked the Registrar to adjourn the examination tint!' Clare and Ridgway, also questioned the bank- rupt on behalf of petitioning creditors.—Mr. Brow°. asked the bankrupt whether it did not occur to hire when he handed over Mr. Rathbone's unfinished house to Mr. Pemberton that he was securing Mr. Pemberten for money lent previously.—The bankrupt said the money was lent conditionally that he handed over till contract to Mr. Pemberton.—The Registrar adjourneu the examination to the 2nd of October.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse held the inquest at St. Helens, on Monday on James Green, of 40, Wellington-avenue, Sefton Park, Liverpool, who was killed on Sunday Morning at St. Helens Junction Station. Green was forty-one years of age, and for about thirty years he had been in the service of the North Staffordshire Railway Company, and worked a train between Burton-on-Trent and Edgehill. On Saturday night at eleven o'clock the train left Burton, and worked its way along to St. Helens Junction, where it arrived at 8.20 a.m. on Sunday. div.head: LOCAL EDUCATION.
div.p: LOCAL EDUCATION.
TECHNICAL INSTITUTE AND PUPIL TEACHERS' CLASSES.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION LAST EVENING.

The Gymnasium was the scene last evening of the prize distribution in connection with the Technical Institute and Pupil Teachers' Classes. There was a large attendance of pupils and persons interested in local educational matters. His Worship the Mayor (Mr. J. Charlton Parr) presided and he was supported on the platform by Mr. F. Monks, J.P., Mr. Alderman Bennett,Mr. Alderman Monks and Mr..J. Moore Murray (director of education).
THE MAYOR ON THE IMPORTANCE OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

The MAirog remarked that he felt it to be his duty as Mayor to lend what assistance he could to the new institution just starting into life—if he might so express it—as well as his personal interest in all that concerned the welfare and the advancement and the reputation of their town—especially from the educa- tional point of view. (Applause.) They woul4 all remember the opening of their Technical School by the Earl of Derby and he (the Mayor) wished his lordship had been pressnt to recognise the good work the school was prepared to do and the efficient and capable staff of teachers that had been provided by the active enterprise and able discrimination of the Education Committee—(applause)--backed by the co- operation and liberal assistance of the town. He felt Mr. Monks was to be congratulated upon the very good start that had been made, and he was also very pleased to welcome the director of education (Mr. J. Moore Murray) to whose untiring energy and tactful management the committee were much indebted for the systematic arrangement of the education curriculum. His worship then proceeded to emphasize the vital importance of education,:especially technical education. He did not concur with the gloomy and pessimistic view that our commercial supre- macy was passing:away, but he felt that if we were to maintain the supremacy we had so long enjoyed educa- tion must be maintained at a high level (Applause).

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

Mr. J. MOORE MURRAY presented the report, in which the numerous changes brought about by local circumstances and necessities and the passing of the Education Act were alluded to. The results of the Queen's and King's scholarship examinations attained by the Pupil Teachers' Central Classes were given, and it was stated that the results must be gratifying to the Committee, and reflcted the highest credit on Miss Warburton, Mr. Buxton, and the teachers of the classes. It was only to be hoped that the progress already secured would be continued under the management of the Education Committee. Last Christ- mas for the first time the pupil teachers were presented for the Cambridge Local Examinations. Twelve passed the senior examination whilst twenty-four passed the junior. Four students of the classes sat for the matri- culation examination of the London University and two were successful in passing. Mr. Murray alluded to the great advantage which the preparatory course at the Technical Institute would be to 'students who were not sufficiently qualified to attend the technical classes. The percentage of passes in the examinations in connection with the Technical Insti- tute (Art. Science, City and Guilds and Commercial) was not quite so good as in the previous year but the nnmber of students who had passed in the higher stages was greater Two students obtained honours in Practi- cal Chemistry, in in Cotton Spinning, one in Short- hand and two n Book-keeping. MR. MONKS AND PASSIVE RESISTANCE. On the motion of Mr. J. DEWHURST, seconded by Mr. JACKSON HOLMES, Mr. Monks was cordially thanked for distributing the prizes. In responding, Mr. F. MONKS said this was at least his fiftieth year of interest in educational matters. He knew there were very great objections on the part of some people to contribute to the Education rate pa conscientious grounds. He had a very strong conscientious objection to sup- porting a lazy man, and therefore he might very properly refuse to pay his share of the poor rate. (Laughter.) He honestly believed that the step which had been taken was one in the right direction, and although he did not approve of the Act in its entirety— far from it—he would do his best to work it in the interests of the youth of the town' and he would trust to future generations to put right what he could not put right himself. (Applause). Alderman MON`KS proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and said he felt that nothing whichhad been dons for many years would be of such vital importance to the future prosperity of the town as the work of the present Education Committee (Hear, hear.) Mr. FULTON SMITH seconded the motion which was heartily carried and the MAYOR briefly responded.

The Examiner, Saturday September 5, 1903. LOCAL WEDDINGS. Perkins—McCandlish Many friends in Warrington and district will read with pleasure of a wedding which took place on Thurs- day morning at Onchan, Isle of Man, in which great interest was centred. The contracting parties were Mr. George Perkins, formerly of the firm of Pattison and Perkins, drapers, Bcc., Sankey-street, Warrington, now of Kingsleigh, 0-rove Park, Ratlimines, Dublin, and Miss McCandlish, late of Blackpool, now residing at Alberta-terrace, Onchan. The officiating clergy- man was the Rev. S. A. P. Kermode. The bride, who was charmingly attired, was given away by Mr. Higginbotham, and *as accompanied by iliss Lily Marsden as bridesmaid, both carrying lovely bouquets, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. G. Harbourne, of Dublin, discharged the duties of best man. The happy couple afterwards left for Llandudno amid the hearty greetings of many friends, They were the recipients of numerous presents, amongst them being a handsome marble timepiece from the Dublin staff of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company, of which Mr. Perkins is the assistant manager. In order to show a further taken of respect, a congratulatory telegram was despatched from the Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School, of which Mr. Perkins was the superintendent prior to his removal to Dublin.

div.head: MEN. THE COMMITTEE'S POLICY.
div.p: MEN. THE COMMITTEE'S POLICY.

Before distributing the prizes Mr. F. MONKS addressed the students. He said that when he was asked to distribute the prizes he hesitated, mainly on the ground that it was difficult to find anything new or interesting to say when all were expecting to receive the rewards of their labour, but the circumstances were somewhat different from the ordinary routine. We in Warrington were passing through a time of distrust of our public men which would lead to changes in almost every depart- ment of public work and the retirement of some who had hitherto done good work in the cause of education and the good government of the town. We were passing from the old to the new conditions in the edu- cational machinery of the town. Hitherto many of our elementary schools had been badly managed, with a teaching staff in some cases inadequate to the work and badlytrained. Considering the nature of the changes and the extent of the work to be done efficiently, he did not see how it was to be done without a consider- able expenditure of public money, with a consequent increase of the rates. If the town expected an effi- cient system of elementary, • secondary, and technical education with a well-trained staff of teachers and a well organized system of training the young to fulfil the position of teachers in the future, they must be prepared to spend the money that would ensure such results. (Hear, hear.) The present Education Committee was accused of extravagant expenditure by those who knew little or nothing of the work that was to be done or the means by which efficiency without waste of time and money was to be attained. The Edu- cation Committee fully realized the responsibility of their work both in the administration of its finances as well as its organization for the discharge of its duties to the elementary schools and also in providing a secondary school for those waiting to take advantage of the opportunity it would afford for the higher education of the youth of the town. (Hear, hear.) But the committee were not indifferent to the requirements of the pupil teachers for better methods and a higher standard than had hitherto been possible under the old voluntary system. Therefore they recog- nizedtheir duty to the teachers themselves by providing a course of lectures •on the theory and practice of teaching, to be given bysome member of one of the leading universities of the country. By those means they hoped to be able to raise the standard of the teaching staff to one of greater efficiency in order that the scholars might be taught the best methods of acquiring the knowledge that was so requisite for their future progress. (Applause.) The experience gained in working the technical schools had taught them that the want of a thorough systematic course of mental training was one great drawback in the work of technical instruction, and until that was remedied they would not realize the full advantages of their technical school teaching. Whether they would be permitted to continue the work so well begun remained to be seen. They would be quite content to bejudged by results, and if the efforts of the committee failed to meet with the approval of their fellow townsmen there would not be the slightest difficulty in making way for such changes as they (the townspeople) might desire To his young friends (the students) was given a great opportunity which he hoped they would not be slow to take advantage of. But they should never forget that there was no easy road to the acquisition of knowledge. Only by steady, hard work could they gain the desired result. They would find it the same in every walk of life, with this difference—that it was easier to the mentally well- trained mind than to those who had not had the. 'advan- tage of a systematic course of mental training. For that reason the Education Committee were anxious to have the most efficient and best-trained staff, and to equip the schools with methods and appliances in order that the students might receive the best training for the various duties they might hereafter be called upon to fulfil. div.head: Birtles—Jackson.
div.p: Birtles—Jackson.

Notwithstanding a pitiless f.downpour of rain on Wednesday afternoon a large number of people trudged along the muddy lanes of Padgate . to witness Ithe marriage ceremony at Christ Church, where the nuptials were solemnized of Dora Eva, daughter of IMr. Thomas Birtles, of Brantwood, Fearnhead, and Legh House, Warrington, and Joseph Foster Jackson, 'son of the late Mr. Joseph Jackson, of Calder House, Garstang. Two o'clock was the hour fixed for the ceremony and by that time the Church was well filled the congregation chiefly consisting of the , fair sex to whom a wedding is always an interesting event. Whilst the wedding guests were arriving the organist. Mr. F. Blackwell played several appropriate voluntaries on the organ, including the Bridal Chorus from " Lohengrin ' by Wagner. The service was fully choral and the singing was capably led 14 the surpliced choir. The Rev. W. Pollock-Hill (vicar of Padgate) conducted the service assisted by the Rev. G. Vale-Owen (curate-in-charge of Orford). Thel service • commenced with the singing of the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" and im- mediately at its • close, the bride was seen walking along, the carpeted aisle, lean- ing on the arm of her father. She looked exceedingly pretty in a dress of white duchesse satin, with veil surmounted by a wreath of orange blossoms. She wore a pearl and diamond necklace,the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by three bridesmaids,namely the Misses Kittie and Lily Birtles (sisters of the bride),and Miss Dorothy Browne (niece). They wore cream voile dresses with fichus of white chiffon, long sashes, rose pink picture hats with chiffon strings. Each bridesmaid had a gold signet ring the gift of the brideatsroom,and they carried choice shower bouquets of pinkroses. , The bride was given away by her father. Mr. Stanley Wright diScharged the duties of best man. During the service, Psalm 128, and the hymn "0 Father all creating" were sung. At the conclusion of the ceremony, the wedding party proceeded to the vestry to sign the register, and afterwards walked down the aisle to the familiar strains of Mendelssohu's "Wedding March." A reception was afterwards held at Brantwood, the residence of the bride's father. About 100 guests attended, including Mr. George Jackson (brother of the bridegroom) and Mrs. Jackson, from America. The honeymoon is being spent in Devonshire. The bride's travelling dress was a blue cloth costume and white felt hat.
