div.head: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
div.p: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
PUBLIC MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
Interesting Speech by the Rev. J. Hirst
HolloWell.
THE REV. J. F. MATTHEWS READY TO GO
TO PRISON.

A public meeting convened by the recently-formed Warrington Citizens' League, which has for its object the offering of passive resistance to the Education Act, was held in Golborne-street Baptist Church on Thurs- day evening. There was a good attendance presided over by Arr. W. Balmford (president of the league). Others present included the Revs. J. Hirst Hollowell, of Rochdale, J. F. Matthews, and 11. Dunnico, and Mr. W. Clatworthy (secretary and treasurer of the league). The proceedings opened with the singing of the hymn "0 God our help in ages past" and prayer was offered by the Rev. J. F. Matthews. THE ORIGIN OF THE LEAGUE:

The SECRETARY in explaining the origin of the league, said rather more than a month since a few passive resisters known to each other met together to consider if it appeared advisable to organise a Citizens' League After careful consideration it was unanimously agreed that it was and they forthwith constituted themselves a nucleus was, which to develope the movement of which that meeting was an expression. For an apology they pointed to the nearly 3,000 summonses already issued, the more than 50 sales of their fellow resisters' goods already affected, and the numerous leagues already formed and said "We follow in their train." The local league now appealed to those pre- sent to use their suppirt, and trusted that after the eloquence awaiting them, many would decide to throw in their lot with them and so make the league a powerful instrument in the town. Dual forms for either full or associate membership were in the seats and they would be glad to receive them filled in either at the close of the meeting or by sending them to the secretary. ' LETTERS OF APOLOGY. THE REV. W. MASON AND MEDIEVAL ' NONSENSE.

The Rev. W. 11 tsoN, of Culcheth, wrote :—" I am afraid I shall not be able to be present at your meet- ing on Thursday evening to which you have so kindly Invited me, so I wish to send you a word'of sympathy with the objects of it. You do well to keep the matter before the eye of the public and to let daylight in upon the iniquities of the Education Act passed by a.Parlia- ment drunken with militarism, and that had no mandate from the people to touch education at all so far as my memory goes. I have.een a teacher in day schools or Sunday schools well-nigh continuously from the year 1852, and I am convinced that the late John Bright was right when he said young children could only be taught the simplest truths of religion, such as "love of God, love of truth and duty, and love of their neighbours," with profit. To teach them such foolish doctrines \as transubstantiation, baptismal regenera- tion, Mariolatry, and other medieval nonsense at the ratepayers' expense is a gross injustice as well as an insult. To tell Nonconformist children,as some of the paiestlings do, that it is a sin to go to a chapel is an impertinence, and as far as I am concerned such teachings shall not be paid for by me. Your day of meeting—Cromwell's day of Crowning mercies' (September 3)—ought to be one of success for your movement."

Mr. ANDREW SCRIVEN. wrote enclosing asubscription but regretting that as he was not a ratepayer he could not take a full pledge. Nevertheless his symnathies were entirely with the resisters and he should do his utmost in endeavouring to get "this iniquitous and do- testable Education Act 'repealed. THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. STRONG CONDEMNATION OF THE ACT. A DISSENTING GRIEVANCE AND A GRAVE CIVIL INJUSTICE.

At the commencement of his address the CHAIRMAN referred to the death of the Rev. A. G. D. Gee, who, he said, had promised to be with them that night and had fromthe outset of the movement been a very cordial supporter. Continuing he said he did not think it re- quired many words from him to justify the holding of that meeting. It had occurred to him that there might be some reason for those who were standing aloof from the movement to hold a public meeting to justify their position. Nonconformists were in danger of forgetting what called them into existence and why they continued to exist. The Act of Uniformity in 1662 made the terms of subscription such that Bishop Sheldon said that had , the Puritans conformed they would have been knaves, and sooner than do so two thousand of the worthiest and noblest ministers in the Church were ejected, and the Presbyterian, Independent, and Baptist Churches word calledinto existence. The Act of Uniformity had to be followed by other and more rigorous Acts, such as the Conventicle Act, the Five Mile and the Test Act, and so now with the Education Act of 1902, either it must be fought and defeated, or other Acts must be passed more unjust and humiliating to Nonconformists, and more dangerous to the State,making not only he ad masterships in schools but even citizenship depend upon churchmanship. For his own part he was inclined to think it did not matter very much what happened, the result would inevitably be the same, for as the Act of 1662 created modern dissent, so the Act of 1902 would hasten on the disestablishment of the so-called English Church. The Act had been.well described as a civil measure with a denomin- ational purpose. Thus it was not only a dissenting grievance but a grave civil injustice, an injury to the state and all its citizens,and it could not be too strongly emphasised that to dissent from the English church was not to forfeit citizenship within the English state. He need scarcely say that that movement was primarily a religions movement though it was quite true that it had both their political and civil sympathy. They were taking that stand because their consciences would not let them do*otherwise and those men who told them that the movement was a silly piece of Nonconformist hysteria, and that a little manly treatment of it by the rating authorities would soon tire these aspirants for cheap tinsel crowns of painless martyrdom, only dis- played their ignorance of the men and the movement and to him this was a happy augury for their success. These rights had been bought at the price of blood and they could not 'sacrifice them at less than cost price. They were not unmindful that religious strifes had ever been the bitterest, the keenest, and often the bloodiest of fights, but till's was a fight they had not sought. It had been thrust upon them. They had sacrificed and agreed to compromise,until now they had been compelled to resist, and readers of history well knew what had always been the result when priestism and power had been opposed by liberty and freedom. Unfortunately the resisters were not as yet very strong in Warrington, but still stronger than many might think. Some from reasons which could not be understood, had not joined the ranks of passive resisters, but he was hopeful that many more would, by the sheer force of circumstances be compelled to throw in their lot with them, and that the political party which professed to stand for liberty, freedom and justice would find that this was a force to be reckoned with and not to be treated with cold indiffer- ence. The different religious bodies in the town which, from whatever reasons, had not seen fit to fall into line in that great national movement for justice, cruth,and religious liberty would have failed in the day of their trial. In Cromwell's time those men were called betrayers of the liberties of England. The Act might or it might not be worked in Warrington on broad, conscientious lines, just alike to Church and State and Nonconformists, but it was not a local matter. It was national, and thus their duty as citizens and NOncon- formists should be plain and straight. They were adopting that method on the advice of some of their, best men both in Church and State—Dr. Fairbairn and Mr. Chamberlain, Dr. Clifford and Mr. A. J. Balfour, and if these men were unconstitutional, illogical and immoral they (the resisters) were not ashamed of at least one half of their advisers —(laughter)—and they were taking that stand as Dr. Fairbairn had said, because they knew the worth of liberty to the people. They had by endurance bought for themselves the right to think, to utter, to argue freely, and they must tell Parliament that at whatever cost they would not, suffer a law which was so grievous a wrong to the dumb and the innocent to continue en- forced and unrepealed. They did not wish to divorce religion and education. They recognized that religion was the essential part of their highest and best educa- tion. The speaker argued that droning of articles,repe- titioris of liturgies and all the cash and contrivances of Birmingham and the Bank of England could not br-ing heavenly fire into a human soul and quicken it out of earthly darkness into heavenly wisdom. Soul was kindled by soul. To teach religion the first thing need- ful and also the last and the only thing was finding a man who had religion and not the man who had attended Communion once in twelve months and subscribed to articles and dogmas he might or might not believe. Because they believed this Act to be doing a grievous injustice to the State, a crippling and cramping of the rising generation, a violating of the consciences of Christian people, they had been

compelled to adopt a measure distasteful to them,which they would gladly find an excuse for not taking if they could, and they asked those present to help them either by joining their ranks as active or associate members. They-were not asking for any favour, only for justice; not for concessions as though their Nonconformity were a sort of civil and political eccentricity for which the legislature ought to make kindly allowance. They asked for it no consideration, nor offered for it any apology.. (Applause).
AIiIiiiESS 'BY THE REV. J. HIRST
HOLLOWELL.

The REV. J. HIRST HOLLOWELL said they were met to consider and to carry out passive resistance. (Hear, hear). Passive resistance required men and women to carry it out and he hoped he had the honour of addressing the very people who meant to do it. Certainly he was one of those who meant to do it (Hear, hear). The chairman was another a.ndhe expected there were others in the meeting (Hear,hear). What kind of an Act'was it under which they refused to pay a sectarian school rate? They objected to the act alto- gether. Under this Act what amount of money was the nation asked to find for sectarian schools ?—Seven and a half millions every year. That was rather a large item. Out of the seven and a half millions,two millions were expected tolcome out of their pooketslas the rate- payers of England. He advised them to keep their rates in their pockets rather than spend them on sectarianism (Hear, hear). What kind of authorities were to dis- tribute these rates if they were paid ?—Authorities they never elected and the members of which were co-opted by Councils some of whose members had already been co-opted. The people were not allowed to elect a single member of the 333 Balfour-education authorities that were being set up. The first thing the act did was to sweep out of existence 2,560 educational authori- ties that were elected by the people. In Warrington they had never had a School Board.. That had been their own fault. They had been playing with clericalism and now it had got its hand at their throats. The Act reduced the number of education authorities to 333 and they might guess what balloonanthorities these were. Some of these authorities had one thous- and scho.ols to look after. Of course the authorities could not look after them. The promoters of the bill wanted authorities that would hand over the money without looking after the schools. In Lancashire they had an elementary education committee, but not a single member had been elected by the people to sit on it. This committee had decided that the sectarian managers ought to pay the salaries and the accounts. Xhe committee had hundreds of thousands of pounds to pay every year and they had' decided to leave the clergy and the sectarian managers to handle that vast sum of money. The electors had to raise the whole costsand the church parson had to }mad over the money to the teacher and pay the accounts. He (Mr. Hollowell) contended that if the County Council raised the money, the officers of the County Council ought to have the payment of every penny. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the County Council would reject this astounding proposal for which Archdeacen Fletcher was mainly responsible. If it did not he hoped the people of Lancashire would reject those who voted for it. (Hear, hear.) Then again they refused to pay rates for such managers of schools as were authorised by the• Act for denominational schools. Out of the six members who were to be appointed not one was to be chosen by the people for that purpose. There were two outside managers put on on the co-option principle. Let them look at what was done at Liverpool. Two Roman Catholics from the outside were added to four Roman Catholics inside. That was giving the people more representation.- (Laughter.) Rev. J. F. IVIATTHEWS: The same thing was done here.

Rev. J. HIRST HOLLOWELL: Warrington is the same. Proceeding •he said the same procedure had taken place in the Church of England schools at Liver- pool. Two sectarians from the outside had been added to four sectarians inside. (Laughter). What about the inside people. In the Roman Catholic schools they were absolutely at the mercy of the Bishop of the diocese. Not one could sit without the consent °tithe Roman Catholic Bishop. He held in his hand a copy of the draft final order refer- ring to Latchford St. James's Church of England school. It was no different from the other orders for the 12,000 Church of England sthools. The order laid down the mode of appointment of the four foundation managers. The first manager was to be ex-officio, and was to be the clergyman of the parish.. Then 'this person was allowed to nominate the second manager. This was what, Mr. Balfour humorously called popular control. (Laughter.) Two other managers were to be chosen, by the present sectarian managers. One of the qualifica- tions was that the person appointed had to have a bene- ficial interest in the parish, which was to be equal to a life estate in land. (Laughter). Last but by no means least, these foundation managers had to sign a declara- tion, its las their pradece sors had to doamder the;old Test and Corporations Act, that they were bona-fide members of the Church of England. As Nonconformists they refused to pay a rate for sectarian schools whose managers are chosen on sectarian, snobbish, and unpopular grounds. The speaker proceeded to state that they further objected to having a rate levied upon them for paying' the salaries of teachers whom they were not allowed to appoint. Mr. Hollowell quoted from a letter written bythe Vicar of St. Helens to a teacher applying for a situation in which the Vicar stated that if the candidate was able to satisfy him on elie preliminary and essential condition of being a mern- ber of the Church of England then there would be very little difficulty in the matter °filter appointment. If the rev canon, continued Mr. Hollowell, paid the salary out of the funds of the Church of England then there would be no cause 'for complaint, but all the salaries of teachers were found by the electors aad they had a right to make the appointments. (Applause.) In referring Ito an argument brought forward by the National Society of the Church of England that the Church of England , only got twenty minutes' use of the schools ancgall the rest went to the nation, Mr. Hollowell pointed out that the Church of England did not give the buildings to the State, they kept possession of them. They also used them for their own purposes on Sunday and week-nights, and this alone was worth at least £500,000 a year to the Church of England. In a passing reference to the establishment of a. secondary school at Warrington, Mr. Hollowell asked why did not Warrington rise to the level of the United States and open free secondary schools to the people. Ho w were poor people to pay ninepence per week? Workingmen were paying for education through the rents they paid and were entitled to have their children educated with- out paying fees. Alluding to the advantages which the sectarian schools received by the new act, Mr. Hollo- well said they had the privilege of making the " atmosphere " of the schools, which was sometimes very heavy with the cobwebs of ritualism. (Hear, hear.) they kept that atmosphere through their power of punishing Nonconformsts by excluding them from the teaching profession. As Nonconformists they declined to pay rates for schools that were carried on for national education and controlled by persons who were determined to maintain sectarian tests and dogma. Mr. Hollowell called attention to a Church of England Magazine called "The Dawn of Day." .

The Rev. J. F. MArenEws said-it was circulated at Latchford. The Rev. J. HIRST Hor.Lowm.r. observed that in the January number there was a story in it which he declared to be revolting and blasphemous. The story propounded the doctrine that a child was nota Christian unless it was baptised, and young women who were•en- gaged to Nonconformist lovers were warned to abandon them unless they would join the Church of England. The story concluded with the statement that if the child which had died had been baptised, the mother would then have known that the child had gone home to its Saviour. Against the dissemination of such doctrines they as. Nonconformists • were strongly opposed. They denied the moral right of the State to lay rates and taxes upon the community for sectarian .purposes. institutions, officials, and tests. He denied the right of the State to lay a rate upon the community for a Con- gregational, Wesleyan, Baptist, Roman Catholic, or Anglican institution. The Act meant that their religion was insulted every day at their expense, that they were disqualified from public offices and had to pay for them. The moment Parliament dictated to •conscience it over- stepped the limits of its jurisdiction. There was a limit in the sight of God to what a free nation ought to take from Parliament. They need not take tyranny from king or Parliament. The civil govern- ment had no right to endow any sect, to favour any sect or to insult any sect. They stood there that night to \ challenge the moral competence of the Government to invade the realm of conscience and to lay a rate on Lancashire for RomanismAnglicanism,or Nonconformity. There they stood. and they stood on an impregnable footing. Sectarianism was not the business of the civil power. Let the sect pay for sectarianism and let the ' nation pat, for national education. Referring to the combination by which they were driven to passive re- sistance, the rev, gentleman said the Bishops of the Church of England and the Cardinals of the Church of Rome were trying to crush Nonconformity. The late Cardinal Vaughan said the Education Act was to be a triumph over Nonconformity. rho duty of loyalty tO conscience, continued the speaker, was higher and superior to the duty of submission to the civil power. They protested against paying rates when the object was to incorporate ritualism and Ronmnism with the civil Government of the country, to put them upon the municipal budget 'of Warrington, of Lancashire and every county. They were being asked to recognise the promotion and propagation of sacerdotalism as one of the objects of municipal government in this country. That was a conspiracy against all government. They were resorting to passive resistance as the shortest argument with the clergy. It was'no use arguing with them in the ordinary way. They were inaccessible to argument and men had been arguing with the clergy for 400 years and never get anything out of them by doing so. The only way.in winch they could get any- thing from that party was by taking it, and they were going to take their liberties with both hands but at the same time not destroy their's (the clergy's). If they submitted to the act it would be the first of a series of woeful oppressions and reaction, The act was not the completion of the clerical programme. It was only the opening of it—the first instalment. What were the other items on the programme? A Roman Catholic University at their expense—the establishment of Roman Catholic religion in the country side by side with the Church of England which did not materially differ from it. They must try

and kill the programme at the start. If they submitted: to the Act as Nonconformists disastrous consequences would ensue. Mr. Chamberlain supposed that the Ties- tion of preferential tl.riffs was going to swallow up the education questi6Fn.: Not a bit of it. Birmingham was quite off the rails in that respect. They did not intend that the fiscal question should be forgotten. God forbid ! If it were a question of intercepting the bounty of God on its . way to the starving millions of England they would light the battle of the poor as they did in the days of Cobden and Bright. (Applause.) They would take both campaigns and fight them together. That was what they did at Argyll. (Applause.) It would be so ,at St. Andrew's, and in other constituencies. In conblusion the speaker said that if they passively resisted they would be following in worthy footsteps. They would be following those who resisted the Act of Uniformity. the Conventicle Act, the Five Mile, Test and Corporation Acts, and the Quakers who would not pay the Church rate. They would also be following in the wake of the abolitionists of the United States who would not obey the fugitive slave law, and by so doing kept the law of Christ and broke, into fragments the iniqnitous law of the States. They; saved their own souls and saved the character,reputatiod,, and destiny of the mighty Republic of which they, were the foremost citizens. (Loud applause.) THE REV. J. F. MATTHEWS WILL NOT PAY.

div.head: PREPARED TO GO TO PRfS6.I•7.
div.p: PREPARED TO GO TO PRfS6.I•7.

The Rev. J. MATTHEws, who was heartily received, announced his intention of speaking briefly although his friendiMr.Hollowell had by no means exhausted all that could be said against the infamous Education. Act. Referring to the story in the magazine mentioned by Mr. Hollowell the speaker said he could confirm it from his own experience. When he was a country parsmi mothers frequently came to him and said the clergy- man would not bury their babies because they had not been sprinkled, and asked him. if he would bury them. Ithad brought tears to his eyes many a time' to think that a Christian clergyman following in the wake of the Master would not bury a little baby because it was not. sprinkled. He had told the mothers that he would cer- tainly bury the children, and without, any fee. He had felt so seriously and profoundly about. the Education Act that this would be the last time that the magistrates would have the oppor- tunity of ordering a distress warrant on .his furniture.. He should tell the magistrates, if they would give him the opportunity, that he should have all his goods and . chattels made over to his wife and he would not be mulcted a single fathing for an Act which was against his conscience. If he was to have. fourteen days in prison he would go to prison. ,He would not, . even compulsorily pay for the Act. How dare he. as a Baptist minister, as a Christian man • out of loyalty to his . God? He left the Church of England from comicientions convictions.. It was his ambition to become a Church clergyman, • and all the prospects that lay before him he threw up for the sake of conscientious convictions. Did they think,,at the beginning of the twentieth' century, that he was going to pay a rate for the endowment of Anglicanism, Roman Catholicism, Wesleyanism or any other ism in. 'Warrington or any- where else? He dare not do it,.he would not do it, and there was no court that would make him do it. (Loud applause.) The meeting then closed with.the pronouncing of the Benediction. .

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Rugby Football. The football season opens to-day with the crash battle. There have been a few preliminary encounters. already, but the campaign proper is entered upon this. afternoon. Warrington are. fortunate. iii being. employed at home, and with such keen rivals as Leigh for visitors, they should draw • a good crowd to. Wilderspool. Leigh have already been in the fray, for they engaged St. Helens on Tuesday in the West. Lancashire League, and were beaten on their own, ground by five pints to. two: Burgess, I note with-. out surprise, was injured twice during the game, and finally retired. Leigh ought tO lose again to-day, atatt if they do their prospects for the South -,West Lancashire trophy will be exceedingly small by the end of the first week in the . season..

Warrington have already tasted the bitters of misfortune. Just when there seemed an excellent prospect of puttihg 'a tip-top tea ra in the field„, the. blow fell. Harris„ playing in. a practice match on Saturday, broke his collar-bone,, and will in conse- quence bean absentee for five or six. weeks. He was playing with great dash—rather too much. for a practice game—and has suffered heavily. The accident placed the club in a dilemma, wilich- they have, got out of by giving the vacantposition to Brookes, who is at any rate excellenthin the defence.. We shall have. to look for points from the other wing, and particularly Fish. The full team, as selected, is as follows : Hallam, full-back; Fish, Isherwood,. Dickenson, and Brookes,"three-quarters ;. Davies and Edmunds,, hail- backs; Thomas, J. Swift, W.. Swift, Cook, Boardman, Morrison, Naylor, and Edmondson, forward's..
It will be noted that for the first time, I believe, in the Club's history, both the half-baek are Welsh- men. They are a smart pair, too, and cmght to keep the men behind busy.

The." A. " team will have an opporttmity of trying the twelve-aside game against Leigh “A" At Leigh with the following team : Knight, fall-back;: •Watkins, Mahoney, and Short, three-quarters ; Jordan and Hardmau,half-backs ; Forster, Lunt, Coleraau, Harmer, Warburton and Roberts, forwards.

• The following other first league fixtutes will also take place to-day :---Batley v. Salford; Broughton. Rangers v. Leeds; Hull Kingston Rovers.v: Halifax; Hunslet v. Wigan ; Keighley v. Runcorn; Oldham v. Hull; Swinton v. Huddersfield;anol Widnes v.Bradford.

Secretaries of football clubs would do well to con- sult the catalogue issued by Frank Suggi 32., Lord- street, Liverpool, before purchasing. outfits and tackle. I have received a copy of this handy publication which gives full particulars of the firm's splendid stock. Having purchased cotton goods, such as material for making shirts, and knickers, before the advance in prices Mr. Sugg is selling to the public at the old prices, thus giving them the benefit of his judgment. All goods are guaranteed. It is impls- sible to refer here to all Mr. Sugg's specialities but 'attention is drawn to the " Football king " which, has been used in international matches, the English-cup semi-final, and all association cup ties,

Leigh on Thursday night selected the following team to oppose Warrington ;,—Pearson, full-back; Ganley, Bennett (captain), Johnson, and Neville,three- quarter backs ; Molyneux and Burgess, half-backs ; Boardman, W. Roberts, J. Roberts, Shaughnessy, Blackburn, Webster, Clare, and Kelly, forwards. The injury Burgess receivad on Tuesday evening against St. Helens fortunately turns out to be only slight, but Riley, a forward, was severely cut over the eyes.

My readers will, I am sure, be specially pleased to learn that the presentation to the hon. treasurer of the Club, Mr. Thomas Pernberton, in recognition of 21 years' valuable service will take place on Tuesday, .September 15th, in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- ttreet, when the proceedings will be in the nature of a "smoker," enlivened by the Warrington Eutt.rtain- .ing Society. The iresent will take the form of a. solid silver tea and coffee set on' :in oak tray with ' solid silver mounts, and will, of course, be suitably inscribed. .
By the way, Mr. Pemberton was busy up to nine o'clock last night selling season tickets, which are going like hot cakes.
Cricket and Angling. . Great pressure on our space this week has com- pelled us to omit the usual notes on Cricket and angling.

div.head: Homing.
div.p: Homing.

The following case ,110111,1 ,orve as a •warning to those who.possess guns and are inclined to use them in the shooting of pigeons : Reuben Shuker, farmer, Lawley Bank, was charged at Wellington, Salop, with_ shooting a homing pigeon, valued at 305., belonging to James Smith, Stoke-on.-Trent. The prosecution was undertaken by the National Homing Union. The de- fendant admitted the offenceiand as he had been previ ously cautioned, he was ordered to pay :£1 9s. includ- ing costs and the value of the bird. He said he would shoot his own birds in future.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

• The season is fast dr-awin4.l; to a close, but local wheelers will not look back upon it with any marked degree of satisfaction. There have been so many dull and wet days that club runs, on the whole, hare not been nearly so successful as had been anticipated. On Saturday only halfa dozen members of the War- rington C.C. made the journey to Cranage. The weather was bright and fine but there was a pretty strong breeze. Tuesday evening's run to Crouton attracted only eight members.

The Lifeboat Saturday Demonstration is being entered into with great zest by locql cyclists, and a splendid turnout is hoped for to-day that is, if the weather is anything like favourable. Mr. E. Pickava,nce, jun., the esteemed secretary of the Warrington C.C., has rendered valuable service in making the arrange- ments for the cyclist section. Of course "Pa" Davies; has also been to the fore,the promoters of the demon- stration readily availing themselves of his experience 41. ycle parades and similar functions,

div.head: BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.
div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.

It is seldom that any discovery of science is such as will benefit all classes of people. Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly oeneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time, injured Other thousands. Even some of the best medi- cinal preparations, however muoh they may do to remove one class of disease, or suit some constitutions, at the 'same time either deepen the hold of another disease, or leave it entirely untouched; or if they benefit one class of patients, they may injure another. Now the great need of the age is some scientifically arranged preparation which will cope effectually with the prevalent diseases of this country, which will be certain to do good when fairly tried, which will be equally adapted to the needs of the mer- chant and the workman, the professional man, and he who wins his bread by the sweat of his brow, the student, the clerk, the factory hand, the miner, and the roadside labourer. It should be, too, such a preparation a contains no injurious ingredients, and which may be taken with impunity by the weakly child, or the delicate lady, as well as by the stronger constituted man. Such a discovery would deserve to be called The Perfection of Medicinal Preparations, and would indeed be an Invaluable Boon to Suffering Humanity. Now this much needed boon has been found, has been tried, has been proved, and wherever proved, it has been found satisfactory. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

HEANY SF.NTENCE ON A. PROFESSIONAL THIEF. Nine mmiths' imprisonment was the sentence inflicted . on Mary Robinson, described as a professional thief. who appaared at the Police Court on Thursday. She was chareed with stealing fron the stall of John Upton, in the Market-place, on Wednesday, one pound .of tomatoes, of the value of 7d. ; from the stall of John Fletcher, two silk bibs and a muffler, of the value of 45.; and from the stall of John White, a blouse of the value of is. 9d. She pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable stated that at a quarter to ten on Wednesday morning, Detective Barlow and P.C. Sankey were on duty in the market and were informed that the prisoner • was hanging about Mr. Upton's stall in a suspicious mintier. Prisoner was known to Barlow, and when the latter asked her what she had under her cloak she dropped a number of tomatoes, one of which was identi- fied by Mr. Upton as his property on account, of the peculiar shape of the stem. Prisoner was taken to the Police Station. Knowing something of her career -Detective Barlow went back to the Market-place and near where the prisoner had been standing were found the other stolen articles, she having obviously dropped them. She subsequently admitted having stolen them. She was a professional thief and shoplifter and began her career of crime in 1883. She had served numerous terms Of imprisonment.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for threa months on each charge—nine months in all.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs T, Birchall (presiding), J. W. Hayward, and S. Wright and Councillor Thornton. VAGRANCY.—For sleepinn, out in an outbuilding at the rear of Paradise place, dolborne street, on Sunday morning, Mary Roy lance, of no fixed residence, was sent to goal .for a month. AN INCOMPETENT SCOUT.—John Moston, 37, Admiral street, Joseph Taylor, 13,4dmira1 street, Fred Bwrgess,7l Wellington street, and John Stirrup, 5, Admiral street, sere summoned for playing pitch and toss at the rear of Admiral street, on August 24th.—?. Cs Wise and Sweeney proved the case. It appeared that on seeing the constables the defendants bolted but 111oston was overtaken and the olicers obtained the names and addresses of the other defendants. Burgess had been acting as scout but evidently failed to give warning of the approach of the police, for Moston was heard to say to him "You're a nice man to be looking out for the bobbies."—The Chief Constable said it was generally very difficult to catch gamblers as they employed more I careful sentinels than Burgess.—Each defendant was , fined ss. and costs. MISDIRECTED INVENTIVE GENII:S.—The following were fined ss. and costs for making use of obscene language.—Elizabeth Lythgoe, 26 Dallam-lane, and Margaret Solan, Margaret Kelly, Annie Towey and Margaret McGrath, all of Foundry-street.—P.S. Evans proved the cases and handed in slips of paper contain- ing examples of the language used.—The expressions used by the last-named defendant called forth strong elnunenti from the Chairman.—The inventive genius displayed in the last case was bad enough, he said, but this example was something wonderful. IM PR ISONM ENT FOR WIFE ASSAUM—William Bailey, Orford-street, was charged on a warrant with assaulting his wife Alice Bailey, on the 23rd ult. He pleaded not guilty.—Mrs. Bailey said that on the above date her husband came into the house under the influence of drink, and commenced to thump her. He also kicked her on the head and discoloured her eye. He gave no reason for doing so.—Prisoner alleged that the •marks were caused by his wife's falling against the bedstead.— The Chief Constable said the prisoner had a very bad record. He had already had three months for com- mitting an aggravated assault on his wife, and on that occasion a separation order was granted.—The bench decided to send the prisoner to gaol for two months, and ordered him to contribute ss. a week to his wife under a separation order. • TCESDIY.—B3fore Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hutchinson, and Dr. Fox. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—For making use of obscene langnage in Ship-yard, Joseph Boyle was, on the evidence of P.C. Phillips. fined ss. and costs. BOYS IN TROUBLE.—James Corbett (13), 4, Union- street ; John Tandy (W. 23, Dolman's-lane; and John Walsh " Crown and Sceptre" Hotel, Buttermarket- street " were charged with stealing from a stall in the Market Place a quantity of plums of the value of Is., the property of William Missey.—The Chief Constable stated that at 8.20 an Monday evening the stall was secured in the ordinary way by the manager,Wm. Ellison, and a number of hampers of fruit were left beside the stall, sheeted, boarded and roped in conformity with the regulations laid down by the Markets Committee. At ten o'clock, in consequence of complaints received, Constable Clough was on duty in the Market Place in plain clothes anl saw the defendants near the stall. The hamper had been rifled, the board, sheet and rone having been taken down, and the boys were helping themselves to the plums. When the odicer approached defendants ran away, but ultimately Corbett was caught and gave the names of the other boys. On being visited at their homes by P.C. Clough and P.S. Williamson' each of the boys admitted having been concerned in theft. Defendants had hitherto borne unblemished characters, and were the children of the most respectable parents—The magistrates fined each defendant 2s. 6d.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. BirFhall (presiding), and
Alderman Hutchin 4011. _ _

A FATHER'S 11;.--G-I.ECT.—John Mitchell was charged with neglecting to maintain his child, whereby it be- tme chargeable to the Warrington Union.—Mr.Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians, said the prisoner left Warrington in July last year and the child had been in the Workhouse for twelve months.—Prisoner, who had been previously convicted, was sent to gaol for two months.

THlMsDAY.—Before Mr. Charles White (presiding) and ' Mi. James Hepherd. RF,FRACTORY PAupErts.—Thomas Brown and George Rlwe were sent to gaol for seven days for refusing to psrforni the task r of allotted to them as casual in- mates of the Union Workhouse on Wednesday. • OBSCENF LANGUAGE.--For having made use of obscene language i the Market-place on Wednesday night, Robert Flannery was fined ss. and costs. A MON"rfl PØR THEFT.—Mary Clarke, Ship Yard, was sent to gaol for a month for §tealing, a carpet bag,
Prudent

containing a table cloth, three pillow cases, and some clothing, of the value of 55., from the Market Vaults,on August 29th, the articles being the property of Elizabeth Bradford, wife of an ironworker, residing in Pierpoint- street.—On Saturday night Mrs. Bradford sent a man named Webb to redeem the articles from pawn. He went for them and on returning stopped at the vaults fora drink, putting the bag on the floor. The prisoner came in, had a glass of beer, and then went out. After her departure the bag was missed, and the police were informed. On Wedtiesday Detective Barlow and Sergeant Williamson saw the prisoner wearing a stolen shawl. She had given other articles to a woman to dispose of. FRlDAY—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Coun- cillors John Roberts, and Thornton. and Mr. Hepherd. IMPUDINT THEFT.—TLIOMOS Clarke, a stranger, was ' charged with stealing from a common lodging house in Stanley-street, a pair of boots, value 3s, the property of William Kenny, a farm labourer.—Prisoner went to bed on Wednesday night leaving his boots under the kitchen table. On coming downstairs next morning he found • the boots had gone and the remains of a pair of boots. which were quite useless, had been substituted. Subse- quently he saw prisoner wearing the boots in Bridge- ; street 4,nd informed P.C. Wise who arrested Him.— Prisoner, who said he took the boots in mistake, was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

div.head: SILVER-STREET DAY SCHOOL.
div.p: SILVER-STREET DAY SCHOOL.
Mr. E. J. Guest and Mr. C. E. Parker
on the Education Question. DISCOURSES BY DR. BEET.

Anniversary services in connection with Silver-street Day School were held in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday. Financially the object was to-clear off a, debt of about £5O, the deficit balance on the enlarge- ment scheme of 1900-1. The late managers of the school made themselves responsible for the financing of this scheme and appealed for hearty co-operation in remov- ing the financial liability. Beyond this deficit balance, the trust is in debt to the extent of swim hundreds of paunds. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. J.A. Beet, D.D., of Richmond College and formerly of the War- rington Wesleyan Circuit. Large congregations as- sembled and the discourses of Dr. Beet were greatly appreciated. The subject of his sermon at the morn- ing service was "God is Love." Love, he said, was a disposition which prompts us to draw others to our.: selves that we may enrich them. Love always sought to be mutual. God loved a lost world because He saw there His own image and saw its capacity for being saved and its capacity forsaving itself. Had there been no Eernal Son there would not have been Eternal love. Love e esr sought objects to love. God resolved to create later-born sons to surround the Eternal Son, whom He would not be ashamed to call brethren. For this reasoa He formed the earth in which His new-born children might be taught the love of God. From the love of Gad sprang the :creation/ of the world. If man had not been free to fall he would not, have been free to stand. Jesus of Nazareth promised endless life in the presence of God to all who believed in Him. For those that re- jected Him there remained nothing but utter and hope- less ruin. This brought us to say "Our God is a consuming fire" (a fire of Infinite Love). In all our dealings with God, the preacher continued, let us remember we are-dealing with infinite love. If infinite love came in it would come as lord and master and would enter every private place and would turn out all that was vile and hateful. Thus there could not be hatred in anyone who had the love of God. A special choir composed of children attending the day school sang a number 91f-quirts very sweetly. Mr. Councillor Upson, the laeadamster, conducted and Mr. B. Wadsworth presided at the organ with his usual *linty. The choir sang the anthem "Glorious is Thy 'Name" (Mozart.) A musical service was held in the afternoon at which the children again sang. Mr. E. J. Guest (secretaryand treasurer) presided and an adchess was delivered by Mr. C. E. Parker, of Penketh. The choir sang the anthems "0 God when Thou appearest" (Mozart) and "0 worship the King" (Nichol). The solos in the first named anthem were sung by Mrs. Parkinson, Miss Lucy Evans, Mr. Hannan and Mr. Perry, and Mrs. Parkinson also sang the solo in the second anthem. The song "The Holy City" (Adams) was effectively rendered by Mr. Hannan. ADDRESSES ON THE EDUCAVON QUESTION. The CHAIRMAN said Olt" believed in the education of the children in the higikst definition of the word. Child's:a needed to have their minds drawn out, and have power imparted t-.) them in order that they might be fitted for life's work and prove themselves worthy citizens in the future, and that they might contribute to the material, moral, and spiritual well-being of the community in which they lived. Wesleyan Methodismhad not de at very generously with day school education. The voluntary contributions by means of which the money necessary for the carrying on of the schools had been ob- tained had come from outsiders rather than from Metho- dists,a/though they had one or two generous contributions from Methodists. The only reason—and he had been told this by employers in the township—that they had con- tributed to Silver-street school was because they might avoid a school tate. Now the Education Act had been passed, and they had a school rate in the town, • it would be moreand more difficult to induce onesiders to centribute to the school., There were some who imagined that now the Act was passed, voluntary con- tribution would not be required. That was a mistake. In the past they had struggled along on something like a year voluntary contributions, and they would want more than that if they were to maintain the school as a Methodist school. The question was as to whether they would continue it as a sectarian school, or hand it over to the authority. Personally. it was not a very gr.t matter' to him. There were a,great many people who aid Silver-street School had been a burden on the Church,but he did not think so. There were some wt.° said day schools were not used for the production of Methodism. It had never been the intention of the teachers to make the children into little Methodists. It had done good, and a very great amount of good. There were citizens in the town who had passed through that school who acknow- , ledged that the Education received from Silver-street had fitted them for their arduous work. With regard to the Education Act, he should like to say that it was looked upon as an Act of great injustice to Nonconformists. He did not think they would feel it so much in Warrington. He believed the Act would be worked here on broad and conscientious lines. But there were some places in the country where the Nonconformist would feel the injustice a great deal more that they would in Warrington. It was their bounden duty as Pree Churchmen to do their utmost to get as many representatives as possible in favour of national education in this country. He had no doubt the Act would work better than a great many of them feared it would. He had spent a great deal of time on the committees and sub-committees, and he was con- vinced that the Act was going to do a great deal for Warrington so far as education was concerned. He thought it possible that many of the schools would find they could not get voluntary contributions, and so the schools would. be handed over to theauthority. Thus ' in future the Act might cause an approximation to a national system of education. He devoutly hoped that would soon take place. Mr. PARKEt delivered an address, in which he stated that these anniversaries in so far. as they deepened the '1 interest of the parents, the teachers, and the Church in the work of the education of the future citizens of this beloved land of ours, were of incalculable service. He I purposed saying a few words about the development of English education. He could not go back to the ' beginning because he did not know where the beginning of English education was, but if they went back to the ' 16th century they found a landmark in educational pro- gress. This was the age of Francis Bacon. Now before Bacon's time, almost all learning was founded upon authority. The church was the sole custodian or truth. Learning was looked upon as the special and exclusive heritage of the Church and the priests. The province of the laity was to work and fight, the pro- i vince of the Church was to conserve knowledge. As might be expected from such custodians, this know- ledge was limited mainly to religion mid the super- natural. The studv of nature was neglected or treated as unimportant. Science was little known. Truth, or what was supposed to be truth, depended not mon faith and reason, but upon the authority of the Church and therefore the attitude of the student towards that truth was not that of comprehension but of acceptance ' and obedience. The mind of man was -thus kept in bonds, and among the indications of the bursting of these bonds was when Francis Bacon in the sixteenth century . began to reason from the facts of nature, and pro- pounded the system of inductive reasoning, as opposed to the authoritative and deductive. Henceforth man began to throw off the bonds of tradition and to exer- . cise a freed reason, in collecting facts and experiences, and feeling for the great natural laws and truths which governed these facts. A greater man (Bacon) had said , "The truth shall make you free." But the echo of Pilot's question had come down the ages 'What is truth ?" The whole truth we mieht never know, but Bacon had at any rate shewed mankind the right way of seeking after truth. Now since his time the history of the growth of educa- tion was characterized by two main features :-Ist, The passing of education out of the hands of the Church 'and the priest into the hands of the laity of the state and 2nd, The shifting Of the basis of truth from -authority and tradition to that of fact, reason and law. Now of the first, they found that education did not stand alone in its divorce from ecclesiastical control. There was a time in the history of England when the Church dis- chsrged many important functions which had since been Nloneyback soap—Fels-Naptha taken over by the people of the State. At one timethe : Church had the charge of the poorand of the sick. They • L ls no other; be no could easily realize how this gave an opportunity to abuse power, by making conformity to the will of the clergy a condition of relief, and so this word in time nther. also passed over to the people and the State. The administration of wills and many other things oS a like No other dares to be moneyback, nature, weren't one time' under the control of the Church. Trip to Frodsham. The members of Sharp-street Primitive Methodist Mission had a trip to Frodsham on Saturday. The outing was organized by Messrs. Harrison and Barrett, two of the Sunday school workers, and their efforts met with success. A. start was made from the Mission Room at about 1.30, Frodsham being reached shortly after half-past three. The members strolled about the village, aad afterwards climbed the hills, while the juniors enjoyed themselves in donkey rides and the swing boats. At five o'clock a capital tea was served, and then amusements were again indulged in. At 8 p.m., the return journey was commenced, War- rington being reached shortly after ten.

ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASs MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Unique Walking Sticks. "The Strand AAgazine " for this month contain a photographic reproduction of four walking-sticks,made by Mr. J. Bancroft. of Warrington. It will be remem- bered that these sticks were exhibited in the window of Mr. Alf Taylor, boot dealer, Horsemarket-street. One stick is composed entirely of penny postage stamps compressed on a steel rod and then turned and polished, another of half-penny stamps, and a third of "Captain Webb" matclit boxes, and a fourth of ordin- ary grocers' sugar paper. The stamp sticks took Mr. Bancroft three years to make, the greatest difficulty being in collecting the stamps. Since the photograph was taken His Majesty the King has expressed his pleasure in accepting the stick made • of penny stamps.

A united meeting of the four courts comprising the Warrington district of the Ancient Order of Foresters was held on Monday, evening in the club room at the White Bull Tun, Horsemarket-street. The chief busi- ness of the meeting was to hear the report of the dele- gate (Bro. W. Bullock) who attended the High Court of the Order, held at Sheffield. the first week in August. Bro. R. Thornley (sub Chief Ranger) pre- sided, and commented on the good fellowship which existed between the various courts in the ^district. Bro. Bullock, in a lengthy address, spoke of his ex- periences at Sheffield, and detailed the vast amount of work got through by the large number of delegates. Several of the members present, including Brothers Thornlev, Hipkiss, Davies (district secretary.) Ban- croft, "grayling, and Walsh entered into an animated discussion, and it was eventually unanimously decided to thank Bro. Bullock for his lucid statement of the business of the High Court, which he had so slily put before them. .

PUOLIC BENEFIT. UNDER the CLOCK BE3T for BOOTS in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Local Oddfellowship. The annual gathering of the Warrington and Manchester district of the Manchester Unity Independ- ent Order of Oddfellows took place on Saturday, and, fortunately, the weather was fine.. The .Manchester brethren arrived at the Central. Station at 1.50 p.m. After partaking of light refreshments at the Blue Lion, Market-place, the party drove through Padgate, Fearnhead, and Newchurch to Croft, wheie an excel- lent knife-and-fork tea .was provided by Host Mains-. After passing a vote of thanks to the host and hostess, bowling was indulged in, a game being played between Manchester and Warrington, the latter proving victori- ous. At seven o'clock. the conveyances were again. boarded, the return journey being by way of Winwick, and the headquarters, the Blue Lion Inn, were reached at eight o'clock. A meeting was held and short speeches were delivered. _

BASSINETTES AND 111 AIL CARTS in latest art shades.—.l. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Sunday School Teachers' Picnic. The teachers at St. Barnabas' Sunday School had their annnal .outing - on .Saturday afternoon, when a very pleasant time was spent at Chester. The party, accompaniedby the Revs. J. Fl. U. Hollingworth and P. M. Forrest, left Bank. Quay Station bv the 2.15 train. As the weather was beautifully fine a sail up the River Dee formed the chief item of the after- noon's programme.. After a walk through the ancient city the • party made their way to the landing stage and boarded a boat for Eccleston Ferry. On reach- ing.this charming res'lrt, a capital tea was served, and afterwards the beautiful grounds at Eaton Hall were inspected. The sail back to Chester was thoroughly enjoyed. The return railway journey was commenced at 8-50, and Warrington was reached at about 9.20, after a trip which was unanimously voted to have been highly successful. -
UNDER the CLOCK Or GOOD BOOTS.—A.dvt.

School Treat. The scholars attending the Council Schools at Daresbury, Hatton;, Moore, and Preston Brook had their annual treat at ,Daresbnry on Friday afternoon, the little ones from Preston Brook being kindly con- veyed in a lurry by Mr. Henry Whitlow. The children assembled about 2.30 in a &Ad placed at their dis- posal by Mr. Billington of the Village Farm, and here games of all kinds were freely indulged in until four p.m., when an excellent tea was partaken of in the school by over 300 children. Tea was over, the juveniles again repaired to the field for the .usual sports for money prizes, and at dusk a pleasant after- noon terminated with the distribution of buns and sweets to each. Thanks are due to the numerous ladies, including Miss Manes, Mrs. Wynne Jones, Misses Littonond others- who assisted in the prepara- tion of.the tea.

div.head: UNHEARD-OF TROUBLE.
div.p: UNHEARD-OF TROUBLE.

When trouble comes, it comes not siegle handed. rhat's the worst of sickness ; it leaves a trail behind, and what follows is often, worse than the evil from which it originally sprang. An interesting case which bears out the truth of such a statement, was recently enquired into by one of our representatives. Mr. Eli Fellows, Wesleyan Chapel Yard, Methley, Leeds, first had some minor troubles during boyhood. As he grew, these increased, and then pains in the chest, brought on by indigestion, would sometimes seize him with terrific force. He would then be unable to move. "So dia- organised and weak were my stomach and bowels," he said, " that I found it almost impossible to take even the lightest foods. Years of suffering naturally weakened and depressed me, and the low state I fell into brought upon me bon spells of insomnia. At night I would lay. and toss about, unable to sleep; yet so worn out that my pains were to some extent numbed by my Nery weak- ness. Unable to eat or sleep, with a constant pain in my chest and stomach, I feared that unless I could soon find some cure I should rapidly sink into worse dangers. At last, when it seemed almost out of the question that I could ever again recover my former good health, Dr. Morse's Indian Root Pills were brought to my notice. From that day I traced the turning point in my career. A few bottles soon arrested the gradual decay of my health, and before I was hardly aware of it I was once more in as healthy a state as a man could wish to be,and all this I owe to Dr. Morse's Indian Root Pills." They are a positive cure for liver and kidmy complaints, biliousness, indigestion, constipation, piles. dyspepsia, foul breath, sallow complexion, and female ailments. div.head: RUNCORN URBAN couNqm.
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN couNqm.
The monthly meeting of the Runcorn Urban District, Council was held in the Council Chamber of the Town .Hall on Wednesday, Mr. S. Taylor, presiding.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
The Medical °dicer reported that 27 deaths and 43 births had been registered during the month. in the corresponding month of last year there were 29 deaths and 44 births.
LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
The Library Committee recommended that seventy- seven books as per list submitted be purchased. The committee presented the annual report for the year ended 30th June last.
Mr. HANDLEY, in moving the adoption of the recom- mendation and report, said the latter was very interest- ing as showing the progress of the library during the 21 years of itsexistence.
Bisbrown seconded, and it Was carried. FINANCE COMMITTEE. AN INCREASE OF SALARY.

The Finance Committee recommended that application be male to the Public Works Loan Board to lend the sum of £750 for twenty one years, to be repaid by equal half yearly instalments:qf principle and interest, re- quired for Canal street improvement ; and that the salary of Mr. E. Marshall, the secretary and accountant belincreased from £225 to £256 a year. to date from 2nd September, 1903. Mr. Imison'moved the confirmation of the report and recommendations. Mr. Salkeld seconded, and it was carried. THE EDUCATION RATE.

An Order of the Local Government Board issued in pursuance of Section 23 of the Education Act, 1902, making regulations in accordance with whieh the amount that would be produced by any rate in the X is to be estimated for the purposes of the Act was sub- mitted.. Mr. Imison moved that the communication be referred to the Finance Committee so that they would know what sort of a recommendation to make at the time the estimates were framed, Mr. Handley seconded, and it was carried. THE. EXTENSION INQUIRY. A MELANCHOLY COMMUNICATION.

The Cheshire County Council forwarded the following letter :—Chester, August 6th, 1903. Runcorn Urban District Proposed Extension. Referring to the local inquiry held by a sub-committee of the Local Govern- ment Acts Committee of this Council on the 23rd June and 14th ult.,T have to inform you that as a result of such inquiry the sub-committee could not recommend the county Council to issue an Order extending the Urban District as suggested in the memorial, as in their opinion the District Council had failed to adduce suffici ent reasons therefor. The County Council at its meet- ing to-day has adopted such report. I have instructed our County Accountant to forward you a statement of the expecises incurred by the County Council in connec- tion with the inquiry.—Yours truly, REGINALD POTTS, clerk of the County Council. -
The Chairman: the letter.
I suppose there is no need to read
Mr. Imison: We are all acquainted with its melancholy contents. (Laughter).

div.head: GOOD FOR HARVESTERS.
div.p: GOOD FOR HARVESTERS.

Farmers and labourers have had unusuallyheavy work this year in consequence of continuous rains which have beaten dowtt the crops and compelled them to cut by hand. This, in the damp weather, is a sore trial to workers always liable to rheumatism, which disables so many. "I despaired of ever getting anything to do me good," said one of them. "The pain was in my hip and nothing would shift it. It racked me day and night, and I had no desire for my meals. I saw in a neivspaper a report about Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. I sent for a box, and after a few doses the pain began to grow less and to shift about from place to place. My appetite came back, and I was able to sleep well. The rheumatic pains grew less and less, andat last left me altogether.!' Asked if he was sure that it was the pills that cured him, the speaker, Mr. Jarvis, of Morley-street, St. Botolph, Wymondham, replied without hesitation: "There is no doubt. Nothing else that I took did me any good. I reckon they are wonderful." Field workers please note.

div.head: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD IN THE ENGADINE.
div.p: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD IN THE ENGADINE.
Another Golf Trophy Secured.

The Paris edition of the "New York Herald" gives some interesting information under the head of St. Moritz aboutthe'recent Bthannual men's golf champion- ship of Engadine allusion being also made to Mr. Crosfield's "fine play." Thepaper says :—The following comments on the recently ended eighth annual golf com- petition for the men's championship of the Engadine are cu lied from an account sent me last evening at my request by a prominent member of the Engadine Golf Club, who watched the matches. Similar material, he adds, is being sent to the "Alpine Post," which- will account fora possill4 coincidence of phraseology. In the first round Mr. G. W. Sands played a boldand dash- ing game, and was beaten by Mr. A. H. Crosfield by only one hole. Both he and his brother, Mr. S, S. Sands, drove a very fine ball. The semi-final between Mr. G. Depew and Mr. Crosfield provided the best genie of the week. Mr. Depow's driving is deadly straightand abso- lutely refiable,a,ud at all points of the game he is steady andfplays in a cool, determined fashion that makes him a really formidable opponent. He generally oat- drove Mr. Crosfield, but the latter had the advantage in approaching and putting, and this advantage mainly won the match, notably on the first, ninth and thirteenth greens, each of which was done in one less than the "bogey" score. On the sixth green, too, Mr. Crosfield made a full driving-iron shot to within ten feet of the flag, and holed out in three which is one under par,play. The last hole was not played out, but at the seventeenth the score for the best ball was 69, Mr. Crosfleld's individual score being 75 and Mr. Depew's 77. This is quite good for links where the record for the extended course is 78. In the final between Mr. J. A. Butt and Mr. Crosfield, the latter won the first three holes in four, five and three. Then Mr. Bott picked up, but to the ninth hole no high-class golf was shown •hy.either player, Mr. Crosfield going out in 41 and retaining his lead of three up. Mr. Crosfield lost the tenth hole in four, Mr.. Bott taking it with a . very fine three, and hence forward an entire change came over the spirit of the7game, as is shown by the scores for the second nine holes, which follow:
Mr. Crosfleld I. 4 3 5 5 4 33 7-38 Mr.l3ott 3 6 4 4 4 5 4 4 4-38

It will be noticed that the score for the best ball is 32, a record that will not be beaten in a hurry. Indeed, my informant ig willing te lay considerable odds against any of the cracks from England equalling, let alone beating it. But for a careless shot, at the last hole, Mr. Crosfield's sore should have been about three strokes less. I have seen a letter written by another prominent golfer on the subject of the matches, and it Is a pleasure 'to quote from the following :—"The matches were really a goods instance of Mr. Citsfield!s ability to pull off hard fought battles. One of his chief delights is a close game, and until the balls are actually hole no one need be surprised to see Mr. Crosfield's lying dead from the approach, or down in a long put, so deadly ig his short game. Many are apt to call shots of this kind fluky; some of them undoubtedly are, but the frequency with which Mr. Crosfield, when pressed or when occasion demands. will establisha close connec- tion between ball and hole is very irritating to his opponent, amd means golf of a very high order. His victory this year in winning the cup was exceedingly popular. He originally presented it to the Engadine Golf Club, and it has been played for eight years. Four times he has won it, and the Committee very wisely, and with the hearty accord of all the golfers of the Engadine, have decided it shall hereafter have a -per- manentltplace among his many golfing trophies. No man has done more for golfing in Switzerland."

div.head: Fatal Result of Breaking Rules, STRONG REMARKS BY THE CORONER.
div.p: Fatal Result of Breaking Rules, STRONG REMARKS BY THE CORONER.

The circumstances surrounding the death of Joseph Burrows, aged 69, of 42, New Road, Warrington' who sustained fatal injuries at the works of Messrs John Edelsten and Son, pin file, and tool makers' nutsford- road, on Thursday of f Kast week, formed the subject of 551 inquiry conducted at the Police Station on Monday evening by Mr. S. Brighouse, county Coroner.—Mr. E. Draper, solicitor, appeared on behalf of Messrs. Edel- sten, and Major Roe, H.M. Inspector of Factories and Workshops, was in attendance. The Coroner read the police report of the accident. Deceased, it appeared, was employed by the firm, and On the date in question, in company with a Inall named Richard Trigger, he went into the Workshop for materials. Instead of going the proper way, which was up a staircase, they opened a door and went through the well of the lift Which was a much nearer way. They were returning iXI the same manner when they were caught by the lift, Which was descending, and both men were knocked down. Deceased seas trapped by the legs. Assistance was at hand and deceased was immediately released and Tnlveyed to the Infirmary. He was found to be suffer- 'rig from fractures of both legs and died on Friday. It aPPeared that there was a notice posted up in the works • stating that "Filecutters, both machine and hand, are entirely forbidden to remain in or pass through the Mores. Anyone breaking this rule will be liable to a tine of ls, in each case. Filecutters are only allowed to enter the stores when requested by the stores attendant for the purpose of carrying blanks." Richard Trigger, 14, Ellesmere-street, a warehouse- Man, then described the accident. Deceased, he said, e4ne into the stores between 12 and 1 o'clock on Thursday, but he had no right to be there. They both proceeded to the workshop through the well of the lift to obtain some material. When they were returning the PIO was down and witness was about to open it when 14 lift descended and struck them both. Deceased was forced on his knees. In answer to Major Roe witness said he knew he had acted against orders. The Coroner: What are the firm going to do with Are they going to tine you is.? That is their option. tiaT : ankkefeurroner : I should think you ought to be Pretty that you are not sent for trial for man- aollr:4t..er. I don't know whether it is not manslaughter allow on are in charge and -deliberately go and and e another man to do something. You tempt him 1711. atiee 4illl to do it. ..nitness : No sir. I did not ask him to come. thee Coroner : lam very doubtful about it. What is aid Putting of the firm trying to protect their workmen notices up if you go and deliberately break them like this? Juror: Are you in charge of the lift ?—No sir. BjEdelsten explained that a man named George was n charge of the stores. There was no lift Was ias the lift was only used about half an I.2eur Per day. The witness Trigger was a warehouseman In the file warehouse. „ The Coroner again commented upon the breaking of ,ae rule. In regard to the fine, he said it was perfectly ridiculous. "I would discharge them on the spot if I 'were the rnaster," continued Mr. Brighouse. " This man admits that he broke the rule two or three times." A Juror: Is it a common occurrence for workmen to Re through the hoist? Witness: No. The Coroner: There is only one redeeming feature. I:he witness is honest about it, and does not try to Prevaricate. A Juror: I don't think he can be blamed for anything. _The Coroner:' You had better talk it over yourselves. Whatever the jury say I know what I shall say to him at the finish.

• After consultation the jury returned a verdict of Accidental death," not adding any rider. The Coroner addressing the witness Trigger said it was only fair to the firm to say that they seemed to have done everything they possibly could in the matter to protect the lives of the workmen. Major Roe said the lift was particularly safe, considering that it was Only worked by hand, because as a rule hand-lifts were not protected at the bottom. In his opinion the em- ployers were entirely free from blame. If there was any blame it was entirely attached to the witness and the man who had lost his life.

TUBE," TRAMS AND THE "SHORT CIRCUIT.." The awful accident which recently occurred in Paris has again brought to the front the question as to how the " short circuit" can be dealt with. The new elec- tric tramways in London have been compelled to post up bills offering ,C 25 reward. for the conviction of any person creating "short circuits by placing pieces of metal, etc., between the slots. We think in the London tubes there is rather more wood used than is necessary; and in case of fire, the timber being in a thoroughly dry state, would ignite very vapidly. The "short circuit" quickly leads to the motor catching fire, and is, in fact, a continual sourc,e of trouble to the electrical engineer.

CREMATION AND CRIME. It has been foolishly argued that cremation will encourage crime by destroying the traces of it. Evid- ence to the contrary comes from India. A 'Lancet' correspondent tells us that appreciable quantities-, of arsenic were easily detected in the ashes and bones from the scene of a cremation. The loose regulations With regard to the disposal of the dead in India favour he crime of poisoning by arsenic very considerably. When organic matter like human bodies are burned in tile presence of arsenic the alkaline salts which are formed combine with the poison and fix it in the shape of non-volatile arsenite or arsenate. There is nothing yery remarkable, therefore, in the discovery of arsenic, the charred remains of a body to which arsenic had °esti administered.

div.p: A QUESTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY

div.head: CANDIDATES.
div.p: CANDIDATES.

ARE YOU COMING OFF THE FENCE? IT is a noteworthy fact that Unionist candidates and members are refusing in increasing numbers to support Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals. They are clinging to the "Inquiry" fence with the desperation of drowning men. But Free-traders, whether Unionist, Labour, or Liberal, will be greatly to blame if they allow them to occupy this position much longer. The plea of waiting for the "report" of the Government's inquiry is obviously insincere. They hope, by putting off the evil day when they must get down from the fence, to test the value of Protection as an electioneering cry. • Candidates should be asked to make up their minds whether they think Free Trade or dear food is best for the country. Mr. Chamberlain never takes any notice of Colonial opinion unless it happens to be in his favour! But when he is talking of reversing Free Trade we must insist that he shall pay some attention to the unanimous decision of the Chambers of Commerce at Montreal. The resolution passed at this gathering asked that the Special conditions of each part of the Empire, including India, should be considered, and, most important of all, THAT THE INDUSTRIAL NEED! OF EACH COMM UNITY SHOULD BE INQUIRED INTO.

THERE are some 200 Members of Parliament who, acccording to their public declarations, do not know whether Free Trade or Protection is the best for the country. It is really a most extraordinary position of affairs. Here is a question affecting the daily life of the people, the very'existence of our national prosperity, and yet these 200 members do not know their own minds about it. It was, we all thought, settled long ago, and yet these members express most blissful ignorance of the whole matter! According to Mr. Chamberlain, the Empire is going to fall to pieces if we do not abandon Free Trade. According to the Duke of Devonshire, it will certainly fall to pieces if we do! Here are, at least, two clear and decided opinions from Unionist leaders: why cannot the rank-and-file take up a similar attitude? Every member or candidate who is sitting on the fence should be asked to come down on one side or the other.

IT is most important that we should consider not only the volume of trade which a country is doing, but also the conditions of the people. A Canadian paper, the Toronto Globe gives interesting evidence on this point. gays the Globe:

Such inquiries as have been conducted in Canada and elsewhere have been entirely one- sided, and there is a sufficient excuse for that in the fact that no other kind of inquiry is possible. A manufacturer of certain goods is asked whether the tariff on that line is defective, and how it can be -improved. To him improvement means greater profits,. and he cons over many changes that can be made to that end. He may be too wise to ask all he would like, but contents him- self with asking what he sees a chance of obtaining. That is half the inquiry, and there it must, from its nature, cease. The elfect of the proposed changes on the other party to the transaction cannot be dealt with.

The truth of these words is obvious. You cannot expect interested traders to give impartial evidence as to the general results of any proposal which may benefit them. We might as well ask the brewers to report on the best methods of promoting temperance. The Government are in a similar position— they are inquiring as to the best way of winning the next election Mr. Chamberlain 'has made up his mind for various reasons (among which trade and Empire play but a small part), that the best way to win is to attack Free Trade. Although the insincerity of his purpose is evident, we shall have to fight him as though he actually proposed to reverse the policy which has . brought prosperity to the country.

ONE of the points we must insist upon in this fight is that the policy of the country must be directed to the purpose of benefiting the whole of the people and not merely a class. It is a very great mistake to imagine, because certain changes would make a certain industry • more prosperous, and certain manufacturers more wealthy, that such a change would be good for the dountry as a whole. A duty put upon a manufactured article might increase the profits of a single manufacturer by £50,000 a-year. But if that profit was made out of the pockets of the British people, by making them iclay more for the goods in question, the people as a whole would be so much the poorer. The Canadian paper I have already quoted also deals with this question. Its opinion is now enforced by the Montreal resolution which declares that in any inquiry into the resolution, arrangements of the Empire the conditions of the workers should be considered. Says the Globe: The gain of 1,000,000d01. by some favoured interest is set forth and placed on record by statisticians, while the loss of idol. each by 1,000,000 people is ignored as of comparatively little importance. There is no possible method of arriving at the results of a proposed fiscal change in Great Britain or,any other country except by the deductive logic which modern economists affect to despise, but which they have neither re- futed nor improved upon. British politicians must reason from the known laws of human conduct in commerce and industry, for these afford the only reliable guidance they can possibly obtain.

BEFORE the workers of Great Britain con- sent to allow Mr. Chamberlain to put a tax upon any article coming into this country, let them ask one or two simple questions. (1) WHAT WILL HE TAX? (2) WHO WILL PAY THE TAX? (3) WHO WILL BENEFIT BY THE TAX? (4) WHO WILL SUFFER BY THE TAX?

When you have got the answers to these questions, no matter what the reply to question No. 1 may be (that is, no matter what articles may be selected for taxation), we shall find that the replies to the others, if truthfully given, will be as follows:
(2) TRE BRITISH PEOPLE WILL PAY. (3) A FEW MANUFACTURERS, AND POSSIBLY A SMALL NUMBER OF THEIR EMPLOYEES, WILL BENEFIT.

(4) THE BRITISH PEOPLE WILL SUFFER. It is because the great burden of any taxaLion upon the necessities of life must fall upon the general public, and heaviest of all upon the poor, that we must insist upon getting a straightforward reply from every Parliamentary candidate as to his position in the matter. Those candidates are not to be trusted with our votes who will not oppose any change in our fiscal system which increases the cost of tha necessities of life. We may depend that the candidate who will do no more thin promise to wait for the result of the Govern- ment inquiry is trying to delude us, trying to get into Parliament with a free hand to support any mad scheme Mr. Chamberlain may propose.
