lonly questi9n was whether any member should have the power at any time on his own account to inspect docu- ments which were not really in the possession of the committee. In this case the information should be ob- tained from the committee, and if the committee refused ' it the member could have recourse to the council.

Alderatan MONKS pointed out that the circutustatres were exceptional and he withheld the information I ruin every member of the committee. He was reading a re- port with reference to a case which the committee were considering but it was not possible to place all the information before the committee, and he claimed at the time that it did not seem to him advisable,consider- ing the delicate position in which the matter stood and the action which might have to be taken, to make the names public. He, however, put the mater to the com- mittee, and as a whole the members were against di- vulging the names. Only the proposer and seconder voted for Councillor Wilkinson's resolution. Alderman BOLTON ; I voted for it. _ _

Councillor PEMBERTON said that was not the first time Alderman Monks had refused to give him information. Referring to Councillor Tinnion's remarks, he said that if any member of the Council used information which he obtained for his own business or for his own profit, he would be the first to denounce him. If ever he (the speaker) did such a thing,levery other councillor ought to denounce him. Some members of the Corporation appeared to be able to get any in- formation they required—most of them were aldermen and deputy-chairmen of committees. He contended that .every counoillor should have the information.

On a vote being taken the following voted for the motion :—Alderman Bolton, Councillors Pierpoint, Wilkinson' Burton, Barton, Hulse, Dodds John Roberts, Forshaw, Thornton, Pemberton, Lord, Dodds, and Brophy, No one voted against it and' the ret3olntion was de- clared carried.

div.head: COMPENSATION TO BUTCHERS.
div.p: COMPENSATION TO BUTCHERS.

The Health Committee reported the receipt of the following resolution from the Warrington Butchers' Association :—"That a cordial vote of thanks be given to the Chairman and members of the Health Committee for forwarding the recommendation to the Board of Agriculture that butchers Should be compensated out of public funds, for beasts bought bona-fide in the open market and found after slaughter to be infected with tuberculosis' the minimum price fixed by the Federa- tion of Meat Trades being £B.—G. Bo wcocic, president; J. UNSWORTH, secretary." A DEPUTATION To LEEDS. It was resolved at a meeting of the Museum Com- mittee that Councillor Thornton be appointeda member and that Alderman Bennett, Mr. May, and the secretary attend the:annual meeting of the Library Association on behalf of the committee.
Alderman BENNETT proposed the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor DODDS seconded.
Councillor PIERPOINT asked whether the secretary re- ferred to was the librarian and also where the meeting was to be held. _

Alderman BENNETT said the word secretary did mean the librarian and the meeting was to be held at) Leeds. He, personally would be unable to attend and if any other member wished to go he could do .so. The minutes were approved. PROPOSED PUBLIC BOWLING GREEN AT _ VICTORIA PARK.

At a meeting of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Com- mittee, held on August 6th, it waa resolved that the Borough Surveyor prepare a plan and estimate for the oonstruction of a public bowling green and that the head gardener be instructed to report upon the suita- bility of the land near the entrance to the Victoria Park for the purpose. It was resolved that the best thanks of the committee be given to Mrs. Garnett, of Penketh, for her gift of 19 Eucharis Amazonica plants. Alderman BOLTON proposed the confirmation of the minutes and said the committee were of opinion that Victorial Park was the right place to make an experi- ment in 'establishing a municipal bowling green. Councillor PIERPOINT said it was the intention and desire of the committee that the bowling green should be made in the best manner possible. No doubt it might be looked upon as an experiment in Warrington, but it was not so in other neighbouring towns in Lancashire. If the public used the green, as he knew they would, other sites. would be provided. .

Alderman SUTTON said he was not an advocate for bowling greens in the towns for various reasons, but if it was decided to make one the cost would be at least £lOO or £l5O, and to maintain it would cost another £lOO a year. He was afraid it would be rather an inducement to many working men to leave their work and i spend the day at the bowling greens. He thought it would be rather to the detriment than the better- ment of the working classes.' Councillor TINNION : "Get away." (Laughter). .. . .

Alderman SuTroN (continuing) said they had plenty of greens in the town, at the Conservative and Liberal Clubs in tile town and all round, and he did not see the necessity of establishing more. Councillor DODDS expressed the hope that if any offer of medals, ezc., for competition on the Corporation greens was made by any aspirant to or holder of Parliamentary honoursi it would be refused. He thought that would be a most improper thing to do,and if any such offer was made he hoped it would be rejected. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JOHN ROBERTS disagreed with Alderman Sutton. He thought he had rather overstepped the mark in regard to the cost of keeping the greens in repair. He thought .E2OO would make a good green, and for attention, Sm., £5O would coverall that was required. Councillor PEMBERTON supported the minutes awl said he knew that public bowling greens all over Lanca- shire and Cheshire gave pleasure to thousands of working men. He would recommend that the committee pay a visit to Altrincham, where the greens had been laid by the public authority very economically and were kept in order for £5O a:year. The charge for attendance was one shilling per month or one penny per hour. The green was never empty in fine weather. All possible information should be obtained so that they could lay down the green economically and make the experiment a success.
Alderman BOLTON said the committee managed the baths and if they could not manage a bowling green it was time to "shut up:" (Laughter.)

, The minutes were then passed. THE 'UNDERGROUND LAVATORY ATTENDANTS. The Markets Committee recommended that the wages of the attendants at the underground lavatories be increased, the male,attendant from 14s. to' 16s. a week and the female attendant from lls. to 12s. per week. Councillor PIERPOINT complimented the Markets Committee upon this proposed advance in wages. He supposed the business transacted had justified the pro- posal. He hoped that within a reasonable time business would increase to suchan extent as to enable the Coin- mittee to pay these poor unfortunate people a little mere. (Laughter.)
You are coming out next
Alderman -HUTCHINSON : November. (Laughter.) The minutes were passed. THE PRICE OPo GAS FOR MOTIVE POWER REDUCED.

The Gas Committee recommended Unit an extra dis- count beallowed on gas for motive power to consumers using gas engines over two hours daily and not less than 70 days per quarter as under :—Three hours per day. id. per thousand, four hours per day. 2d. per thou- sand, five hours per day, 3d. per thousand, six hours per day, 4d. per thousand. The minutes were confirmed on that proposition. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

RAILWAY COMPANY AND ARPLEY CANNONS. At a meeting of this committee the Town Clerk re- ported that the London and North Western Railway Company had inserted in the agreement with regard to the maintenance of Arpley road a condition that when , called upon the Corporation shall remove the guns I opposite Arpley station. The TOWN CLERK was instruc- ted to inform the Company that the corporation would object to such condition. In other respeots the agreement was approved. It was resolved that three days' holiday be allowed to the employees of the tramways department after 12 months' service, and an additional day for each year after the first year up to a maximum of 7 days; that a special meeting of the Council for the selection of Mayor for the ensuing year be convened for Monday, the ttliat September, at 6 o'clock. The minutes were confirmed. THE PRIVILEGES OF COUNCILLORS. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND THE INSPECTION OF BOOKS, &c. AN INCIDENT IN COMMITTEE.

Councillor PEMBERTON moved:—"That every member of a committee shall be entitled at any time to inspect all the books, papers, and documents of such commit- tee and shall at all times have access to all the works and undertakings of such committee." His reason for doing so, he said, was to put, beyond any doubt the position of the chairmen ef committees towards the other members. At the last meeting of the Electricity Committee a document was read by the Chairman and he asked for two names contained in it. Why the document should not be handed to him he did not know. He contended that it was the duty of the Chairman to direct debate and lay the business before the committee, but he denied Alderman Monks's right to keep any documents or books from him. At the committee meeting he had to press the Matter very much and say that if the informa- tion was not given to him he should take steps to bring the question before the Council. He waited for some time and then Councillor Wilkinson moved a resoluti on that the names should be given to him but no one seconded it. Consequently he (the speaker) had to second the resolution and on a vote being taken three voted for it and the other members remained neutral. He contended that this wasan indignity which members of the Council ought not to stand and every official and chairman of a committee should know that every member of the Council had a right to see any document which came before hie committee. Councillor LORD secondedj because he thought that every member of any Committee ought to have the use of any document which the Chairman had. Alderman BOLTON supported: Every member, he con- tended, had a right to inspect the whole of the books and papers of his committee and to visit the works. In some instances if a man was not the chairman of the committee he was practically ordered out of Corpora- tion works because he was not labelled. Councillor TINNION said he had never been refused any documents which came before committees of which he was a member, nor had he been refused access to Corporal ion works. He pointed out that certain docu- ments might be made use of by members to the advan- tage of their own private businesses, if they felt so dis- posed. He did not think thlt it was desirable that a member should at all times have the right to inspect documents for his own private gratification or gain. He would not put that temptition in the way of any man. If Councillor Pemberton's intention was that a member of a committee whileacting with that committee should be able to see any document which any other member of the committee, including the chairman, had had, it \tato only fair that he should have that right. Councillor DODDS contended that as representing the ratepayers the members of committees had a right to see every document brought before the committees. The MAYOR said there was no question that every member of the committee had a perfect right to see the documents which came before the committee. The

div.head: DEATH OF THE REV. A. G. D. GEE.
div.p: DEATH OF THE REV. A. G. D. GEE.

Although it is onlf'about twelve months since the Rev. A. G. D. Gee took charge of the Emmanuel Re- formed Church, Bold street, he had endeared himself to the members of the church and it was with deep regret that the congregationheard on Sunday of his death. The , rev, gentleman had attended to his ministerialliuties up 1 to about a fortnight ago when he contracted a cold and despite the attentions of Dr. Joseph he gradually became worseand passed away on Saturday afternoon at his resi- denc in Wilderspool road. By his death at the age of 39 years Emmanuel Church has lost a conscientious and hard working minister. The rev, gentleman was a staunch supporter of Protestant principles, and was a strong opponent of Ritualism, about which he was always ready to speak. He was formerly curate of St. Mary's Church, Birkenhead, and was for some time engaged in ministerial work at Westwell, Kent. He was ever ready to sadrificehimself in the work he had so much at heart, and his character was such as to call forth encomiums from the late Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Ryle), by whom he was ordained. He leaves a widow and one child—a daughter. The funeral took place at the cemetery on Wednesday afternoon and many relatives and friends witnessed the last sacred rites. The first part of the service Was held in Emmanuel Church, the Rev. J. Rowland-Parker, of Tuebrook, officiating. There was a good attendance of parishioners. The hymns "0 God our help in ages past" and "Jesus lives', were sung and the Rev. J. Rowland-Parker delivered a short address. He said that by the death of Mr. Gee the church had sustained a great loss. For a very brief time their brother was engaged at that church in the ministry of God's Holy. Word, but he (the preacher) was sure the congrega- tion had learnt to love and esteem him for Christ's sake. He boldly proclaimed the Evangelical and Protestant truth and was an ambassador of Christ sent to glorify Him by preaching the gospel and building up souls in the kingdom of God—As the mourners left the church Miss Lees, who presided at the organ, played the Dead March in "Saul." The chief mourners were Mrs. Gee (widow), Mr. Gee, of Buxton (father Of the deceased clergyman), Prof. W. Gee, of Manchester and Mrs. Gee, Mr.F. Gee, of Man- cheste-, Mr. and Mrs. Harold Gee, of New Brighton, Miss Edwards, and Miss F. Edwards, of London. The members of the church present included Mr.ThomasAllen and Mr. William Dickens(wardons),Messrs. A.H. Landon, T. Gandy, H. Gandy, Smithson, and several sidesmen. The Free Church ministers in attendance were the Revs. John Yonge, G. H. Carnson, R. Wilkins Rees,J. F. Matthews, H, Dunnico, J. S. Hughes,J. L. Milne, J. Gardham Reed, F. Lake-Good, and J. Williams. _ _

In aceerdance with the deceased's last wishes the hymn "Rock of Ages" was sung at the graveside. Many beautiful floral trzbutes were forwarded including one from the congregation of Emmanuel Church, and one each from the young men's and young women's Bible classes.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S OPPONENT.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S OPPONENT.

Mr. W. J. Davis, the secretary of the National Asso- ciation of Amalgamated Brassworkers, who has been chosenby the Labour party in West Birmingham to con- test Mr. Chamberlain's seat, is probably the best-paid trade union official in the country, his salary being over four figures. Mr. Davis has one hobby, the collection of old coins, in regard to which he has written a book; and a year or two ago when his treasures were dis- persed they created almost a record in prices.

div.head: LIVERPOOL INVITES THE KING:
div.p: LIVERPOOL INVITES THE KING:

Efforts are beitig made to get the King to visit Liver- pool, and lay the foundation stone of the new Cathedral on St.James's Mount, early next spring. It is olaimed that Liverpool Cathedral will be the first cathedral erected in the twentieth century, that at Truro being an expansion of a parish church. The Diocesan Commit- tee, which has £175,000 in hand are striving to increase that by £2s,ooo,which is the limit they have laid down, before the stone is laid. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
ANOTHER LONG SITTING.
QUESTIONS AND MOTIONS BY
NON-TRADERS.

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The business engaged the attention of the members for over three hours and at times there were lively passages between them. The Mayor (Mr. J. Charlton Parr) presided, and there were also present, Aldermen Fairclough (deputy-mayor), Monks, Bennett, Sutton, Hutchinson, Bolton, Francomb, Councillors Ellison, Tinnion, John. Evans, Forshaw, William Pierpoint, Wilkinson, Rogers, Hulse, Barton, Dodds, Lord, Pemberton, Horrocks, Thornton, Craik, John Roberts, Brophy, Upson, Burton, with Messrs, J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), S. Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), J. M. Murray (director of education), Dr. Gornall (medical officer of health), F. V. L. Matthias (chief assistant electricity department.)

div.head: TRAM CONDUCTOR SPENCER'S CASE.
div.p: TRAM CONDUCTOR SPENCER'S CASE.

The following motion by Councillor DODDS wasagain on the agenda:—" That the case of Tram Conductor Spencer be investigated by the Tramway and Elec- tricity CornMittee, and that in harmony with the reso- lution of. the Council of the Ist July, 1902, he be allowed to be represented by such person or personsas he may appoint." Upon rising,Councillor Dodds stated that he had been absent for some days and there had been a rather startling development in this case, in con- sequence of which, and as Councillor Pemberton had put a further notice of motion on the agenda, he pro- posed to savethe time ofithe Councillby withdrawing his motion in favour of Councillor. Pemberton's. THE POLICE BUILDINGS. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S MOTION. "HAVING A GO' AT THE POLICE BUILDINGS." Councillor PEMBERTON moved :—That the resolution passed at the meeting of the Council held on the 10th June to pull down the old Armoury and build an Inspector's house be rescinded. In doing so he ex- plained that hia reason for moving the rescinding of the resolution was because it did not express what the Watch Committee themselves wished to do. From the resolution they would be led to believe that they were only going to pull down the old Armoury, and finish the Inspector's house. That he found was not the state of affairs at all. What the Watch Committee intended to do was to complete that portion of the building now used as an Inspector's house also to complete the parade room, which would make it double the presentsize, and further to build an entirely new house altogether. That was never shown on the original plans nor on the origlnal contracts. He thought that this revealed a very serious state of things. In the past they had had too much misrepresentation. In the resolution it was riot shown that they were going to make the parade room double thesis e, nor that they were going to build an entirelylnew Inspector's house. He then quoted an explanation of the Borough Surveyor at a previous meeting with regard to the proposals. He further argued if Mr. Davenport's claim were paid it would result in a net gain to him of £785 us. sd. He under- stood that all materials had been removed from the ground, and that the place was practically finished. With all due respect to the Town Council if it was the intention to complete the inspector's house and build another, he thought the work shquld be re-tendered for. Four years ago the price of building material was very high indeed, and, therefore, it vvat neither right nor fair, as this was an entirely new house, drawn to a new plan, that this contract should be let onthe oldschedule price. The thing he wanted to emphasize most strongly was that everything done in that Council and by the Corporation should be' done in a proper and straight- forward manner. There should be nothing to fear, and every member should be in possession of every fact for and against. Councillor THORNTON seconded.
The MAYOR suggested that the best plan was to ask the Borough Surveyor to explain matters so that they would have a better knowledge of the facts of the case.

The BOROUGH SURVEYOR drew the attention of the members to a plan on the wall i , and explained that when technical classes came into existence n Warrington it was necessary to find them somewhere to lodge, and the only place which was available without a large ex- pense being incurred was the old Armoury. They had now got new technical education premises, and the old Armoury was not now required for that purpose. In the meantime the Police Courts :had never been con- structed on the original lines, and he wanted the mem- bers of the Council and the public to understand that the original plans were passed by the Home Office, and they could not depart from them for the simple reason that they had to borrow money from the Local Government Board to coMplete these premises. Then he pointed out that the parade-room must be made of sufficient size to permit ef the drilling of the number of police that they had to have in Warrington. In addition to that, in the onset the plans approved included two; horses for residential men in connection with the Police Courts, but their proposal was to reduce the proposed original expenditure by about £BOO, as it was found that for the present two dwelling-houses were not required, but only one. In order to do this they must null the old armoury down. If they did not increase the parade-room the Home Office would come down upon them. The old materials were worth something at the present time, and if as a Corporation they did not want them they would sell and realize a good price. It was true that the contract was let to Mr. Davenport, but the adjudication of that contract rested with the architect and not with him. The thing was in embryo. Councillor Pemberton had asked if Mr. Davenport had sent in an account. He granted that ho had, but in the event of that the matter went over to Mr. William Owen, of Warringtoa as their arbitrator. In answer to questions the Surveyor re-. peated that one house only was to be built. In answer to another question he added that the present parade room was not sufficient.

Councillor TINNION said he always likedhavinr, a "go" at the police buildings, and rather . revelleclbin the opportunity of doing so again. (Laughter.) He then pointed out that there was a great difference between the statements of the Borough Surveyor and Councillor Pemberton. He understood Councillor Pemberton to say that what they proposed to do was an entirely new departure from the contract. (A Member: "Certainly not.") From the Borough Surveyor he understood that the plans were sanctioned by the Home Office, and that they did not intend to carry out a portion of thesephins. It seemed to him that they should lei the matter rest where it was or complete it in- a proper manner. The MAYOR. said he understood the Borough Surrey- or's remarks with regard to the parade room were to the effect that the extension would be in accordance with the original plans. Councillor THORNTON asked if there was any request from the Home Office to proceed with the work? - The _MAYOR replied that the plans had originally been passed by the -Home Office, but there was nothing further.

The BOROUGH, SURVEYOR said it was ft-mml by the Chief Constable that he could do with or.o house in- stead of two. Alderman MONKS said the fact that the constables had to pass frequently through parts of tho present Inspector's house had weighed very considerably with him when the amended plans came before the Council some time ago. Alderman BCiLTO'N said he did not think they should cavil at furnishing the block although they had wasted money and made the mistake of having too elaborate a plan in the first instance. Alderman SUTTON suggested that if the matter was adjourned the Council might meet at the Police Court and go into the matter thoroughly. The MAYOR thought this was a wise suggestion, and asked Councillor Pemberton if it would meet his views.
Councillor PEMBERTON said it would entirely. He questioned whether they could complete the parade room, as they had only the consent of the Council to the completion of the Inspector's house. _ •
The discussion was then dropped for the time being,
TWO BIG LOANS.

The Finance and Estate Committee submitted a reso- lution to the effect that application be made to the Local Government Board for the borrowing of the sum of 1-'lO,OOO for the purpose of private street works; and the Town Clerk, at a meeting of the same committee on August 24th, reported that the Board had sanctioned the borrowing of £18,600 for the purpose of electric lighting. On the motion of the DEPUTY MAYOR, seconded by Alderman BEET'', the minutes were passed.
THE LIGHTING OF THE BOROUGH. INCANDESCENT LIGHTS TO BE USED

'At a meeting of the Streets Improvement Committee, a report by the Lighting Sub- Committee was presented on the lighting of the Borough. The sub-committee recommended that the men should start their rounds half-an-hour earlier than at present, mid that four additional lamp- lighters he appointed. The Committee further recom- mended the substitution of incandescent lights for ordinary burners throughout the borough. Several parts of the borough were badly lighted, and it was proposed to rearrange the existing lamps and to provide additional lamps where required. The lighting of the electric poles after midnight was unsatisfactory and e,pensive, and the committee recommended that unless better arrangements could be made the electric light be dispensed with and incandescent lights substituted• Alderman SUTTON proposed the adoption of the minutes, and said it was not intended to force the adoption of incandescent lighting, but simply to recom- mend that it should be carried out, as far as possible, in the main_ streets of the town. (Hear, hear).
Councillor TINNIoN: The vi-hole of them? Alderman SUTTON: Well, the main streets first. CounciIIorWILKLNSON seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor DODDS said that six months ago he asked a question with reference ton lamp being placed at the Sankey-street end of Crosfield-street. He would like to know something about it as his constituents had been

div.head: LIFE STORIES ILLUSTRATED.
div.p: LIFE STORIES ILLUSTRATED.

A NAVAL OFFICER'S WIFE. The career of a naval officer is proverbially a responsible and interesting one. His noble pro-. fession carries him to strange lands and distant shores, and his knowledge of men and the world lends an added charm and weight to his opinion and conversation. His cheery spirits and in variable good health all tend to his happiness, a blessing which he would willingly share with others.

div.head: and wi
div.p: and wi

The dangers incidental to his calling are treated with that indifference which is associated with the highest type of courage, and when a coveted Distinc- tion is bestowed on the gallant officer we can rest assured that it has been more than fairly won. But in the midst of the Honours and Perils of a naval career the sailor may perhaps be haunted by thoughts and anxiety for a suffering wife at home. Here, indeed, is a case in point. The gallant officer, with whose permission we print the letter below, gives in terse but telling phrases his opinion of Phosferine as a remedial agent for gout and ase of his wife. An officer's word is emphatically to be relied on, d that Capt. Carr's letter will be read with the deepest interest.

Capt. G. S. Q. CARR, R.N., C.M.G. (who was decorated for service for various operations against natives in the Nyassaland Protectorate), 25, Burlington Road, W., writes :—"I have pleasure in saying that Mrs. Carr has derived the greatest possible benefit from the use of Phosferine for rheumatism andgout, and purposes continuing the use of it.
"As a general tonic she has also derived great benefit. As we have found so much value from its use you Isave my permission to publish this letter."—May iith,l9o3.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR Th 3 Council and the Education • Committee.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR Th 3 Council and the Education • Committee.

Sir,—Thanks are due to Councillor Upson for his -courageous and trenchant speech on Educational . matters in the Town Council last Tuesday. It was evident from his speech and from the speeches of those who sought to oppose the recommendations of the Education Committee that the latter had signally failed:to grasp the'true value which the engagement of a good. secondary school staff means to the town and were advocating a policy which Iventure tadescribe as one of "False Economy." Would itnot be wiser if instead of further pursuing this policy and thus seeking to hamper the Education Committee, they were to retrace their steps' and support the latter in their well-intended e efforts. of bringing ,Warrington up to the standard of other towns in the . matter of Education? Surely the_y have no desire to handicap the children's future! I know they would scorn such an idea. But it means this, if they persist in their present policy. May I say also that there appears to me to be a sad lack of discrimination on the part of certain gentlemen who have recently entered the Council and in their zeal -to "save the rates," are opposing almost everything. I am (pita Imare that it is the desire of many ratepayers that the Council should retrench as far as possible, but I doubt very much if it is their desire that this should •be carried within the realms of Education. If thdy do then I think not only the children but the town also is • to be pitied for its low -` ideals."—Yours faithfully, ENGLAND.

The Education Act and Passive Resistance. Sir,—Were we a thoroughly righteous people we should it-have wise and just laws; for in that case our rulers would be boiled to carry out the wishes of their con- stituents in all legislation matters. Unfortunately, • however, the golden rule of claim, unto others as we would have them do unto us is -only very partially and obeyed amongst us. And therefore when our legislators inflict injustice upon the people they are no more responsible for that injustice than are the majorities who sent them to Parliament as their repre- sentatives. The new Education Act is a striking case • in point. The Government now in power were re- - turned by an overwhelming majority of the people, and that Act occupies a very prominent place in the programme of their legislative performances. Denomi- national experts allege that the Act inflicts an outrage upon the eeligious freedom of nearly one half of the people of this country. And so strongly do the non- conforming bodies feel the injustice of being called upon to pity for the teaching of religious doctrines • . which •• they utterly detest that large ,num- bers of them are• refusing to pay the Education rate. But I would respectfully submit that this is not a policy worthy of Christian men. There may be tyranny and injustice in the Act; but whoever found anierely human law free from such blemishes? Let me cite a few cases in point. No righteous man could be found to justify the land laws of England which, in the interest of the aristocracy, deprive the great masses of the peopleof their divinely appointed inheritance in the soil ! But where are the " passive resisters " to the demands of the landlord; for rent! %Again, if I may judge the liquor laws by their fruit, then lam bound to say that no more unrighteous and evil-producing enactments were ever set in inotioti by • " the- wit of -man." But I have cover yet heard or read (I.N-he ratepayers banding themselves together to resist payment of the taxes levied upon them for the support of the paupers mid criminals made by intoxicating drink. '-Once more, the late war in South Africa was an outrage upon every principle of Christianity and the rights of , -men. But HO attempt was mtde to stop the supplies for carrying it on, and, so far as I know, no passive resisters" have yet appeared to repudiate their share.of the price of blood. Christian men, above all others, should be consistent in their ways. If their consciences A. permit them to quietly wink at the injustices Ihave referred to, and. others whose name is legion, it smite strange that their souls should be so stirred, as they , appear to be, by the minor evils of the Education Act. And besides, and far above all this, they should remem- ber that the Lord whom they profess to love and obey, has laid it down, both by teaching and example, that his followers should bear and not resist evil.—Yours truly, lONA.

div.head: Stockton Heath Schools.
div.p: Stockton Heath Schools.

.Sir,—Frorn the prominence which has been given to the newcomer question in the Stockton Heath School controversy your outside readers will be led to the . conclusion that Warrington, orat any rate As important southernsnburla—looks with no friendly eyes uponnew- ,-corners, that it. is, in fact, clannish—if not positively churlish—in its behaviour to strangers. As my personal experience is quite contrary to such a conclusion I should like to bear witness to that fact. I have had experience of living amongst people of widely 4ifferent natures-yet I have not found more -genial neighbours nor mere readiness to show a friendly ..-spirit anywhere than I have found. in Warrington. The vicar of the parish in which I happened to fall and his good, wife. wero—very. fittingly, amongst the first to show friendly sympathy. Df course One mustn't expect open arms immediately 9n arrival in a new neighbourhood, or from some people even at all—most folk wart to know you first,-and same even need to look at you -twice, yet thentore,one learns of life the more one finds that the Arid looks 9n yea very much in the same way as you look upon it. 4 smile begets a smile, a frown a frownr-we ,meet many reflections of ourselves in onr ;journey, _ _

Notivithstanding, therefor€' that I was one of the • ‘,7tetccoaster' subscribers to the famous requisition whose boldness called forth the unfortunate remark, I doa't feel hurt because I quite understand the circumstances. • When an advocate's case is a,poor.one and reason is all ~on the other side he may be pardoned if he lets slip an -uncharitable remark which he certainly regrets after- wards. This; I believe, explains the slip which should Aow rest in.oblivion.

That we in;Stockton Heath are not averse to ' out- side ' interference was proved by the subsequent action of the majority at the same meeting. We decided, by ;two to one,that the agitation for tetteraccommodation (promoted by ourselves who knew all about it) was pre- 'nature, and that we ought to wait until some distant .authoritv drew nur attention to the fact. \inch has been said about cost. We must ever be prepared for this objection—at all events front a few persons who ,talwa.ys.object to any expentlitare, yet this objection will ,notprevent justice being done to children and teachers when the true state of matters is realised by the think- ing ratepayers. That the present schools are sadly out .of date, insanitary and inadequate, is fully admitted, :and nothing butoomparison with such schools as are ,unfortanately to be found in Warrington, could have ,excused their existence years ago. What does the "sufficient accommodation" amount to 'which was said to exist until July last but which does .not exist ,now ? Siinply this! that with the present .cubic area per child the sclools were in the worst con- .ditio-n allowatiie by the Board of Education. Surely mot a creditable position! Moreover, theeonclusions of practical :expertc prove that 200 cubic feet per child is 'necessary tor healthy conditions and even then the 'ventilation must be of the beet. On this moderate cal- .culation there are more than trice as many scholars on -the books as the schools are fat to accommodate. This is badenough to justify more than a public meetigg,and I feel sure that ere very long, the majority will join the minority in demanding or.providing schools of which we shall all be proud.—Yours
TW. H. SHERBURN. OraPPeoliall-rd.,StocktonHeatil. 3rd Septernlaer,l9o3

div.head: Examiner, Saturday September 5 1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday September 5 1903

all England for three years, and if that was not a suffici- ent qualification for a secondary school he didn't know what was. The chemistry master soon after his selection got .250 more than the Warrington Committee offered him and went elsewhere, while three other men got better appointments in other towns. Therefore he con- tended that the Warrington Committee were economical on the question of salaries and were also selecting the best men. He did not think the remark which had been made by Councillor Horrocks was altogether justifiable as to the expenses whiCh had been incurred by the managers. At the inception of the Act in April things were in a chaotic condition, and no one knew where he was, yet the schools had to go on anl things purchased. The item to which Ceuncillor Horrocks had referred was a small one. Councillor Forshaw had dealt with the secondary school. In other towns provision was being made for 12 children per thousand in the secondary schools. That was being done all over England, and it was an accommodation upon which the Government would insist. That meant a school of at least 500 ex- cluding the Grammar School. He thought they had killed that matter--the putting of the Grammar School into competition with the secondary school. There was no competition between the two. They were try- ing to provide a good education for the children of the working classes, an education that would perfectly fit them for their future life. If they hada Council of the most rigid economists he thought they would hie corn- polled to do what the present committee were doing. 'But they were not the ultimate authority. Behind their backs were the Board of Education, and it was notorious that the present Board had been very lenient and gentle with the Voluntary schools in time past, but if they got a progressive Government,a Liberal Govern- ment that some wanted, the pressure would no doubt be greatly increased, and the expenditurelon educationlwas bound to go up. The committee had been as economi- cal as it was possible to be. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Bor.ToN said that this discussion had arisen in consequence of Alderman Bennett not having taken the Council into his confidence. He ought to have shown that there was a necessity for all this. There appeared to be a kind of distrust and a belief that the Education Committee were trying all these matters in an experimental manner. But the best men for the positions had been selected and it would be acknow- ledged that instead of a great expense• being involved the secondary schools would earn their own living by the grants. He did not think the Council had anything to complain about. The whole question was new, and he thought the committee ought to be trusted for at least 12 months. (Hear, hear.) ' Councillor PEMBERTON supported the amendment, and contended that the two previous speakers had get hold of the wrong end of the stick. Councillor Upson had made a very impassioned speech, and might lead one to think that he and Councillor Lord and others were the enemies of education—but it was nothing of the sort. Their contention was that the staff was too large for a secondary school, and that Warrington was rushing on in front of other large towns instead of wait- ing and profiting by the experience and mistakes of such places as Liverpool and Manchester. The advertisement 'for' the Secondary school .A appeared for three weeks one after the other in three different prominent educa- tional papers, and if Councillor Upson had been doing his duty he ought to have seen to it and it might to have been stopped. It was not stopped, and seven or eight people were invited to come to the town and three were selected. One of the three had not the quali- fications as a master in a secondary school A. if they were going to have a secondary school A, it was a most natural thing that they should have a man who had had some experience for the purpose. What was alarm- ing the town was this extraordinary expenditure. 4What was it going to amount to on elementary education? Everyone was in favour of education, but there was no reason why Ithey should spend £5,000 if £3,000 would do. He did not know what the masters would do to fill their time up. Then a very small committee had voted this expenditure, and it was time for the Council to put the brake on. A few of the old hands on education were over-riding the new education members. Councillor PIERPOINT said he was a member of the Education Committee, and he had been brought into that position by the Act of the Government and the Government must take the responsibility for his acts. He did not think he should be extravagant, indeed he had always tried to be economical. He pointed out that the question of establishing a secondary school A was brought before the Council, debated, and the principle affirmed; so was also the question of appointing teach- ers, and the power which had been conferred upon the Education Committee had been very properly exercised. 'They had had the benefit of the most expert educationa- lists in Warrington. They might have been extravagant —he was not responsible—but there was .no doubt that up to this point everything the committee had done had , been debated in that Council, and affirmed or rejected. Alluding to Councillor Horrocks' speech he said he had always had a great objection to sweating, and if the Voluntary schools had been sweating it was a credit to the Education Committee that they were putting their feet down and saying that everyone who worked for them should be paid a fair day's wage for a fair day's labour. (Hear, hear.)

" WARRIGTO'N SCEIOOLS MISERABLY

STARVED. Alderman IVlolsncs said Councillor Upson had practi- cally covered the whole of the ground, and had put the matter in some respects better than he (the speaker) could put it, but there was one feature that should be alluded to and it was, namely, the stipulation in the advertisement that the applicants should have had experi- ence in a secondary school A. Ho was not at the meet- ing of the committee when this particular point was considered, but it was in deference to the wishes of the whole of the comaiittee that the stipulation was with- drawn. The committee met on the Monday, the last week in which the advertisements were appearing. The London and oountry journals were going to press on Thursday, and there was little time in which the Di rector of Education could withdraw the stipulation,but after the expression of opinion the stipulation was withdrawn in the interests of the local candidates so that they could have a fair chance. It was not thought worth while to withdraw the stipulation in the country journals but it was withdrawn in the local papers, and in the applica- tion form that particular clause was struck out. Nearly half of the applicants had had no such experience, showing that notwithstanding that the stipulation was put in it was not sufficient to'prevent a large number taking their chance. They were not trying to lead the country, and in that respect Conncillor Pemberton was entirely wrong. On the contrary they were doing very little compared with many places. The Committee were only trying to do the minimum because of the fear of additional expense. It was notorious that the schools in Warrington for years had been miserablystarved with regard to theteaching staff, arrangements and construction of buildings, and with regard ta new and suitable accommodation, and the Government Inspectors had been more reasonable to Warrington than they had been in most places because they had been aware of the difficulties the trustees and managers had had to face. Councillor DODDS thought the discussion had not been wasted. There had been a great deal of dis- satisfaction in the town and it was, therefore, desirable that Councillor Upson and Aldermen Bennett and Monks should make the statements they had made as to how the money had been spent and was being spent. He was in favour of a better system of education. and he should support whatever expenditure was necessary to put the schools on an equal footing with the schools of other towns.

Alderman BENNETT said his fear at the outset was that there was a tendency towards extravagance, but the more he had gone into the matter the more he was beginning to understand the bearings of the question, and the less he was disposed to make that criticism. He was entirely opposed to extravagance, but whatever they starved they ought not to starve the education of the town. (Hear, hear). Councillor LORD eventually withdrew his amendment with the consent of his seconder, and the minutes of the Education Committee were confirmed.

div.head: MO NSTER CHILDREN'S PICNIC.
div.p: MO NSTER CHILDREN'S PICNIC.

I A picnic of over 3,000 children is certainly a novelty ' and quite a stir was created in Warrington on Thursday afternoon when a miniature army of juveniles set off for a drive to Lynam. !‘fr John Maginn, who recently con- tested St. John's Ward without success. offereci to give I a free picnic. to the children of the ward and needless to I say full advantage was taken of his liberality, Teachers and ministers of all denominations were invited to co-operate to make the event a great success, and, the weather being beautifully fine, the children enjoyed themselves to the full. About 3,100 were conveyed to Lymm no fewer than thirty 'buses and • a special train being required to accommodate them. A tractioniengine was also requisitioned to draw four , waggons laden with happy vounr.tsters. Mr. Maginn accompanied his guests in Mr. W. Winstanley's motor car, Mr. SVinstanley driving. The journey to the pretty Cheshire village was accomplished without mishap and the children proceeded to a field near the railway station which had been lent by Mr. Norcott, of Statham. They were free to spend a pleasant hour according to inclination, and most of them indulged in donkey rides and swinging. An excellent tea consisting of bread and butter, cakes, and buns was 'lserved in marquees, the batering being carried out in first-class style by .Mr. Collins, of the Spread Eagle Hotel. A separate tea was served for the teachers and helpers. A hearty vote of thanks was accor- ded to Mr. Maginn, on the proposition of the Rev. D. R. James.—ln responding, Mr. Maginn suggested that a simi- lar picnic should be given each year to all the childrea who did not miss a single attendance at school during the twelve months. He'thought ten gentlemen should take the matter up and he would contribute his share. If the scheme were carried out it would be an induce- ment to children to attend school regularly, the govern- ment grant would be increased, and education in the town would cost very little. He suggested the scheme to local economists in preference to the scheme of false economy in the way of cutting down teaehers salaries—The return journey was accomplished in safety and the streets at Warrington were crowded to witness the children's return.

div.head: COST OF EDUCATION. MORE CRITICISM OF THE SECONDARY SCHOOL.
div.p: THE COST OF EDUCATION. MORE CRITICISM OF THE SECONDARY SCHOOL.
MUNICIPAL PROGRESS.
By J. WILLIAMS BENN, L.C.C.

The recent attacks upon municipal progress have been so persistent and so well financed that some good people who are not behind the scenes are really beginning to imagine that" Municipal Trading," as it is ingeniously called, is really, inimical to the success of private enterprise, and is productive of high rates. To alarm further the timid ones it is labelled Socialism," and the cautious citizen is warned that its encourage- ment may lead to something akin to the Parisian Com- ntune. One's apprehension abates when it is dis- covered that these bogeys are raised by a "League," whose aim it is to exploit our towns and cities for dividend purposes. Indeed, the list, of the members of this anti-municipal fraternity is so signifi- cant that argument becomes almost unnecessary. But I propose to treat this assault on our municipal life quite seriously, and to contend: First, that "Municipal Trading" is really essential to the success of the great bulk of private enterprise; and, second, that it has proved to be the friend rather than the enemy of the overburdened ratepayer. My argument, for the present, does not touch the more important moral and social reasons which are outside these comparatively selfish considerations. As to.the first point, the observant traveller will notice that the success of shops, hotels, and businesses generally is largely measured by the health, attractions, and convenience of the city in which they are located._ _

People, especially those with money,congregate where they can get the best light, air, water, markets, and means of communication. " But," it may be asked, "cannot all these things be effectively and cheaply supplied by private enterprise ?" Fully recognising all that private enterprise has done in such directions, I reply: "Not nearly so well as by municipal action," and for a very simple reason. The common good," as it is so well named in Glasgow, must naturally come second when getting a good dividend is the first con- sideration. Two or three illustrations from London will shew what I mean. It has had to trust to private enterprise for some of its most important services. For tramways it relied, a few years ago, upon thirteen differ- ent companies all working separate unconnected systems, without even the gauges being in common. Certain populous portionslof the Metropolis had been secured by these companies, and the rest, the parts really most in need of development, left severely alone. Thus the congested parts were but little relieved, and the shopkeepers, builders and others have fared badly in the districts which were without tramways. Now, if this service had been under municipal management' it would have been one instead of thirteen systems; it would have been spread over the whole area, and arranged on the principle that "trarnways should precede as well as follow population." The "common good" would have been the guiding principle rather than the securing of an uncommon dividend, and the prosperity of private enterprise in all parts of London would have been greatly enhanced. Again, take the question of the water supply of the Metropolis under eight companies, with varying powers and charges and overlapping areas. Some few years ago there was a water famine in the East End, in con- sequence of which poor people died, and trades which were dependent on water were seriously injured. All this was not because there was insufficient water, but because the company which ran short had no connect- ing pipe with its neighbouring company, which had plenty ! Indeed, there was an ample supply within half a mile of those who were dying for the want of it. Under a municipal system such disastrous consequences would have been avoided, and many thousands of pounds saved to those engaged in private enterprise. To draw other illustrations from London, the distressing spectacle of a fine river without an efficient steamboat service, the docks and port trade in such a condition that they cannot continue without State or municipal help, all shew the folly of leaving to dividend-earning companies certain communal duties upon which the business life—i.e., the private enter- prize of a city—depend. The example of the docks is most forcible. An enormous trade would have been secured by London if the port had for the past fifty years been managed by the municipality or by some such trust as those which are established in shipping cities. Much of this trade has gone to Antwerp or Hamburg. Yet some people say this method is "municipal trading, which must be checked.

IThere are, of course, among such critics many who concede that a municipality may be entrusted with such things as water and, perhaps, lighting, but they object to the building of houses for the working classes as seri- ously interfering with theproper trade of builders and landlords. Let us look at that objection for a moment from the point of view of the bulk of those who are en- gaged in private enterprise. If the latter are to pro- duce or sell their articles at reasonable prices—prices that will compete with the foreigner—they must have their workers somewhere near their works decently housed at reasonable rents. The builder or landlord who is reaping a fortune Out of a house famine in a congested district is doing so at the expense, perhaps ruin, of every other trader in the vicinity. The municipality which in such a case takes the duty of housing in hand, only looking, if necessary, for a bare return of the money expended, is conferring a great boon upon the traders of the district. It is true that the builder or the slum landlord may onffor, but the good of the greatest number—specially of traders—would be secured. lam no advocate, how- ever, for municipal housing schemes which involve a charge on the rates. There should be no charity rents or rate-aided wages. It is needless to multiply illustrations or to say that these cases are common to cities other than London, although the Empire City is the most behind. For these reasons I submit that municipal trading--so-called—is really essential to the success of the great bulk of private enterprise. I may be asked: "What should this municipal trading include?" My answer is: "That must depend upon local circumstances." In some cases it may well include bathing machines, or golf links, or rifle ranges. In other cases such "extras" would be unwise. It should certainly embrace everything in the town in the nature of a monopoly, or having to do with the control of the streets and the public health. The latest returns show that Parliament has per- mitted "municipal motor 'busses" to be added to water, electric lighting, gas, tramways, markets, baths and washhouses, housing, cemeteries, slaughterhouses, and fairs. The decision as to where to draw the line may well be left to the locality cony earned. The system of direct election which nofi- obtains is a sufficient check against any scheme which is likely- to destroy the business of a town. Dealing now with my second contention that " muni- capal 'trading has proved to be the friend of the over- burdened ratepayer," I am able to quote from the return handed in by Sir Samuel Provis to the Municipal Trad- ing Committee so recently as July 17th last. It shows the results of what are described as the 'reproductive undertakings " of the municipal corporations of Eng- land and Wales (other than the London Ceunty Council) for a period of four years from March, 1898, to March 11902. The list includes waterworks, gasworks, ecc., baths and washhouses, burial grounds, working-class dwellings, harbours, piers, docks and quays, and "other reproductive undertakings." The result covers 299 towns and cities having an aggregate population—census 1901—of 13,093,870, and an assessable value-19004-0T £55,076,203. Taking the uhole, the return shows that, after deducting all ex- penses of working, establishment charges, and repay- ments of principal and interest, there remained a net profit of £378,281. This is after, including in the list— absurdly, I think—such undertakings as baths and wash- houses, burial-grounds, harbours, piers, docks and quays. No municipality can expect to make a profit out of necessary public services ; such as, for instance, cemeteries. On these there is a deficit of £175,703, which has been deducted from the really" reproductive undertakings." The amount to the credit of the latter as net profit is, therefore, £653,984. The total capital involved in all these undertakings is £121,000,000, and during the four years named a sum of £16,000,000 has beenpaid off, in addition to the net profit of £378,281. This is a result which should reassure the anxious rate- payer as to his provincial friends, but the critic may inquire why has London been excluded? Curiously enough, the real Corporation of London 'which ministers to its 5,000,000 of inhabitants is called 1 a County Council. This was due to the necessity. of I saving the amour propre of the old City when Mr. 1 Ritchie's Act of 1888 was passed. So we have to rely ion the figures of the Council itself for information. ißut they have been duly audited by the Government : officer. The Council NI only permittedl ati present I to deal with two of the "reproductive undertakings" lin the above-mentioned list, viz., housing of the working 1 classes and tramways. With regard to the latter, the ! total expenditure on capital account on all the Council's ' dwellings up to March 315t,1903,amounteti to £1,221,754 17s. 7d. The total financial result on the whole of the , dwellings and estates from the date of the opening of 1 the first block in April, 1894 down to March ! 31st, 1903, is a surplus amounting to £9,306 2s 7d., after 1 making a net contribution from rates of £12,237 3s 7d. This result has been arrived at after making full pro- vision for repairs and 'renewals, charging interest, on capital outlay,and setting aside a sinking fund sufficient ,to replace the whole of the cipital outlay on land and 1 buildings and estates in course of development within a 'period of 60 years. The sums annually charged against I the various dwellings and carried to these accounts have ' been carefully reviewed by the housing manager, and they represent, in his opinion, a full and sufficient pro- vision for future expenditure under this head, which will naturally be larger in years to come than it is at present, when most of the buildings are almost new. When it is remembered that the sums annually set ! aside for sinking fund purposes, together with interest ;accumulations, amounted on March 31st, 1903, to Atotal 1 of £37,719 165., it will be seen that by the operation of 1 this sinking fund the,ratepavers of sixty years hence will come into possession of an unencumbered freehold i property yielding a large profit income. This has been done in spite of the fact that a large portion of these , dwellings have had to be erected under statutory obliga- tion without regard to any • chance of profit. Last 1 year's accounts show that the total gross income ' for the year amounted to £74,126 ss. 10d., and of this £32,948 Os. sd. was required for outgoings during the year. In addition to this a sum 1

of £35,269 6s. 7d. was required tor the payment of capital charges. There is thus a surplus balance on the year's working of £5,908 18s. 10d. So much for the finance of this sort of "municipal trading." But it is of more importance to recollect that this re-housing of some 30,000 of London workers has kept within the county a large volume of trade, which, but for this timely action, might have been pushed out into the provinces. Thus the private enterprise of the Metropolis has been materially assisted. Finally, Ina)" liturn to the question of the tramways, now so essential apart of the life and prosperity of a city to reassure the ratepayer that he need not be anxious on they account. The total sum spent by the London County Council on tramway purchase is £1,984,983. The first purchase was effected in 1895. Since that time £293,592 has been applied from the same service to the relief of rates, while £176,940 has been paid off the original debt. Thus the ratepayer has been largely benefited by the policy of municipal tramway ownership. But it may be urged that these figures represent the result from lines leased to a company as well as lines worked by the Council. Taking the latter separately—a small system of twenty-four miles, representing only one-fourth of the tramways of London—the total financial result for four years shews a net profit of £79,000 to the relief of rates, a oserve fund of £30,009; and, over and above all this, a number of municipal advantages which deserve to be specially mentioned. These include:

(1) Establishment of all-night car services. (2) Extension of halfpenny fares. (3) Reduction of fares on various routes. (4) Institution of special workmen's services with return tickets at cheap fares, up to eight o'clock a.ra• Further, the Council has improved in various waYs the conditions of labour of the tramways staff, the fok• lowing alterations having been made: • _ _

(1) -Men allowed one Ciay's rest in seven. (2) Establishment of an average ten hours' day. (3) Wages of various classes of employs increasen• The totalannual cost of these changes has been about £26,000, duly debited before arriving at the above annual prat. There are no halfpenny fares, or ten hours a day, or one day's rest inseven without deduction from wages, on the lines which are leased to the Con' panies. Fifty millions of persons are carried on the Council's lines at halfpenny fares. If they travelled on the company's service, where only penpy fares obtainp they would pay £lOO,OOO a year extra in tramway fare This I submit as a useful object lesson 02 real municipal progress, selected from a city which is, alas! much behind most of the municipalities in the provinces. If I were dealing with, say, Glasgow or Birmingham—that centre of light and leading—rouch more forcible evidence would be adduced. Sufficient, I trust, has been said to show the selfishness and hollow: ness of this attack which is being made by interestee people on that resonable municipal development upon which the life and prosperity ,of the dwellers in our cities depends. J. WILLIAMS BENN.

div.head: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.
div.p: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.
To-day's Demonstration at Warringtoo.

To-day's Lifeboat Saturday demonstration promises to be in every way worthy of the town. The officialS have given their time freely and ungrudgingly to make the arrangements as complete as possible and only the cheerful influence of the sunshine will be required t° crown their efforts with success. The people of War rington will, we believe, be only too anxioit to show their appreciation of the work 0; the gallant men who man the lifeboats minim our coasts by contributing handsomely to the funds of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. They ha" the assurance that the whole of the money raised by ala demonstration will be devoted entirely to the paymen° of lifeboatmen and grants to their widows and children' What more worthy object could they be asked to sur port? The procession will probably be quite equal to anything that Warrington has ever seen of that description. As would be seen from the Pr.cr, gramme which we published last , week there 'sc!" be a hest of novel and interesting features. The 11fe boat " Busbie "and crew will figure in the pageant, arnh there will be no lack of music,nearlyall our local ban" having promised their services. The military elerael will be represented by the Volunteer Band, Mounte Infantry and Cycle Corps. Other attractions will be several fire brigades, of Warrington and Lyainll cyclists in fancy dress, harriers in origille; and comical costumes, vehicle tableaux, nu' • * the Crewe' morris dancers. The procession'stS , will assemble round the bandstand in the at 4.30 this afternoon and proceed to the front Parf the Town Hall. Afterwards the following streets wilt be traversed :—Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street, the Irlam-street, Church-street, turn at the lamp peer Parish Church and back, down Church-street, Mersey- street,. Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street, Will"— street, Tanners-lane, Froghall-lane, Priestley-street, Powys-street, Liverpool-road, Bank Quay Bridge, Parker-strpet, Wilson Pat ten-stroet, Bold-streot, Palmyra-square, and Springfield-street to the Park. At eight o'clock a smoking concert will be held in 11: Drill Hall and the proceeds will be added to the parP:". collection. An excellent programme has been draw' up and during the interval the prizes will be dist& bated.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. WIDNES WIFE DESERTER PUNISHED. At Widnes, on Monday, Timothy Kinsella, a local -man, was ordered to prison •for two months for desert- ing his wife andthree children. On April 29th prisoner aeft them destitute. Nothing was beard of him until Saturday, when he was arrested owing to a violent assault on his wife, who had left the workhouse to arrange terms with him whereby they should live to- • gether again. A GALLANT RESCUE. At a meeting of the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society, at Liverpool, a silver medal and vote of thanks were awarded to John Ellis, a workmari engaged on the Transporter Bridge Works at Widnes, for bravely Plunging into the river Mersey from a platform sus- Pended from the new transporter bridge at Widnes on August 13th, and rescuing a child (aged six) who had fallen into the river. CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES SHOPKEEPER. At Widnes on Thursday, Julia Carney,wife of Thomas Carney, Waterloo-road, was charged with exposing margarine for sale without a label. Mr. Knowles de- fended and stated that there had been an oversight on the part of the defendant after cleaning the shop in not putting the label on the margarine. There was no intention to defraud, and he thought justice could be done in the case in ordering defendant to pay costs. The bench took this view of the case, and dismissed it Oil Payment of costs. BETHESDA. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH RUNCORN. The annual choir sermons were preached at Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, on Sunday, by Mr. A. Thompson, of St. Helens. An augmented choir, under the conductorship of Mr. E. Worrall, sang the follow- inganthems in excellent style: "As the haxt pants" (Mendelssohn), "Here by Babylon's Wave" (Gounod) and " By the rivers of, Babylon " (4toot). Mr. George Pritchard presided at the orgam The solo " Behold I stand at the door" was sung by Mr. John- stone. Collections were taken in aid of the choir fonds. CHARGE OF KICKING A WIFE AT WIDNES. At Widnes on Monday morning, Joseph Tarleton, 33, nigh-street,Widnes, was sent to the sessions for trial (3111 a charge of wounding. His wife, Kate, who gave evidence against him, appearea with her head in band- ages, and two black eyes. She said that a woman made some allegation to her husband concerning her. She left the house, but he'afollowed her, and bringing her hack into the house, beat her about the face, and kicked her on the head with his clogs,- causing a wound two iaches long.—Dr. Hutchinson dressed .the wounds, and -said they were caused by some blunt instrument. Upon examination of the clogs, blood stains were found upon them.—Prisoner asked if there were any stains on the of the clog, to which the doctor replied" No."— ..risoner now put the question. "Could the stains on the heel and side have been caused by walking through , I:21e blood?" To which the doctor replied Yes."— -Further evidence was called for the prosecution.—ln answer to the bench if he had anything to say why he hould not go for trial, prisoner replied "twill say nothing." The case came before the manager of the department and the man was reinstated but his character was taken from him. Spencer came into the employ of the Ceeporation with thirteen years' good character and naturally, although he was reinstated, he wanted to retain his character. This was the second black mark he alleged had been made against him wrongfully. He asked, through the Secretary of the Union, for the case to be heard by the committee, but although there was a stand- ing order over-riding the committees in such matters, the committee refused to hear his apnlic,ation. They laid down coaditiOns that the Secretary should hear certain evidence, but this was not agreed to, and he (Councillor Pemberton) could not see why he should have agreed to it, because it made no difference. Since then further charges had been made against Spencer and on the face of them they looked very black, but he contended that before a man's livelihood and a thirteen years' character were taken from him undeniable evi- dence should be produced. Councillor DODDS seconded. Councillor TINNION supported and said the question was evidently surrounded witha great deal of misunder- standing and probably misrepresentation but the man had a perfect right to have his character vindicated and on the other hand the action of the committee might be vindicated to some extent. Councillor PIERPOINT said he did not altogether like interfering with a cOmmittee and its employees but if the Chairman would say he had no objection to the pro- posal, he would feel better satisfied. He had every sympathy with the resolution. Councillor BURTON was of the opinion that the man should have an opportunity of coming before the com- mittee so that they could hear what he had to say. Alderman SUTTON said the man was charged with being incapable of taking charge of a car when he arrived at his work. Councillor PIERPOINT: Was he intoxicated? Alderman SUTTON: I understand he had had some drink at all events and he was quite incapable of taking charge of the car. Continuing he said he understood the committee agreed to see a deputation of Spencer's friends but for some reason the appointment was not kept and the committee considered they were perfectly justified in not giving the man any further opportunity. The alderman went on to complain of such matters being brought before the Council. He never knew in the course of thirty years' experience in the Council so many trivial charges and motions brought forward as had been introduced during the past twelve months. In nineteen eases out of twenty it was proved in the end that the charges had been unfounded. He hoped that the inquiries which were going to be held would end in proving to the public—as he believed they would—tleat if there was any censure at all or if there was any disoredit whatever, it would redound upon those who were con- stantly making complaints without any reasonwhatever. He was quite in agreement with the resolution, but at the same time he said emphatically that it had been the fault of the man's friends that an investigation had not been made and an opportunity given to Spencer to defend himself. Alderman MONKS said that if it were merely a question of Conductor Spencer and that alone he should at once agree to the appointment of the committee but a much larger and a more important question was involved. He understood that on December 25th the man was found at his work in a condition which justified the inspector in suspending him. He was afterwards reinstated and when the matter came before the committee he under stood the members felt it would be a very difficult matter to get at the true facts of the case. Afterwards Spencer wanted two further witnesses to be examined and Mr. Grimsdale gave Mr. Plinston an opportunity of being present.
